title: Provide HashML-DSA
need_summary: The developer asked how to use HashML-DSA for signing hashes, and the answer points to OpenSSL documentation showing how to disable message encoding to create HashML-DSA (https://docs.openssl.org/3.6/man7/EVP_SIGNATURE-ML-DSA/#ml-dsa-signature-parameters).
security_topic: request for HashML-DSA support in Python cryptography
question_text: I need support for HashML-DSA as well.
answer_text: Openssl allows you to manually create HashML-DSA by disabling message encoding (see https://docs.openssl.org/3.6/man7/EVP_SIGNATURE-ML-DSA/#ml-dsa-signature-parameters). It would also be an option to offer this (custom message encoding) in the cryptography module, however, it requires the user to have a bit more expertise to use.
thread_text:
ISSUE #14827: Provide HashML-DSA
Author: mschulz-at-hilscher
Date: 2026-05-08T13:27:41Z
Labels: 
State: open

[c0]
Python cryptography already supports ML-DSA.

I need support for HashML-DSA as well. In our secure boot implementation, we hash the firmware binary and then provide the hash for verification to different digitial signature algorithms. Pure ML-DSA would require to pass the complete data to the hash function, which is inefficient regarding startup times. Just signing the hash with Pure ML-DSA does not make use of the clean context separation provided by HashML-DSA.

Instead of the complete message, HashML-DSA can create a signature based on the given hash of some input data.

According to FIPS 204 (https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.204.pdf), the HashML-DSA sign function consumes a digest as message and the hash algorithm used to generate the digest as additional parameter.

Optional contexts are supported for both ML-DSA and HashML-DSA.

[c1] @mschulz-at-hilscher 2026-05-26T07:08:08Z:
Openssl allows you to manually create HashML-DSA by disabling message encoding (see https://docs.openssl.org/3.6/man7/EVP_SIGNATURE-ML-DSA/#ml-dsa-signature-parameters). It would also be an option to offer this (custom message encoding) in the cryptography module, however, it requires the user to have a bit more expertise to use.

title: AESGCM fails on RHEL9 in FIPS mode
need_summary: The developer needed to know why AESGCM fails in RHEL9 FIPS mode and a workaround, answered with an explanation of OpenSSL provider mismatch and a suggested fallback to Cipher, anchored by commit 98dfafeb8dcdf5e640c9612841f07da66586509b and a cryptography.io documentation link.
security_topic: AESGCM failure in FIPS mode due to OpenSSL provider version mismatch
question_text: AESGCM fails on RHEL9 in FIPS mode
answer_text: After a bit of discussion in #pyca irc channel it looks like the main culprit is that `aead.rs` uses LazyEvpCipherAead vs EvpCipherAead based on CRYPTOGRAPHY_OPENSSL_320_OR_GREATER but depending on the main OpenSSL version. So if a FIPS module uses a lower version (3.0.7 in this case) than the main OpenSSL version, it selects an implementation that only works with the default provider but not with the fips provider.
thread_text:
ISSUE #14795: AESGCM fails on RHEL9 in FIPS mode
Author: schwabe
Date: 2026-05-04T13:43:39Z
Labels: 
State: open

[c0]
Precondition: Have RHEL9 running in FIPS mode and cryptography 46

Small unit test minimal example:

```
def test_aes_gcm_encrypt():
        from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
        import os
    
        key = os.urandom(16)
        aesgcm = AESGCM(key)
    
        iv = os.urandom(12)
>       encrypted = aesgcm.encrypt(iv, b"I am a test", None)
E       cryptography.exceptions.InternalError: Unknown OpenSSL error. This error is commonly encountered
E                           when another library is not cleaning up the OpenSSL error
E                           stack. If you are using cryptography with another library
E                           that uses OpenSSL try disabling it before reporting a bug.
E                           Otherwise please file an issue at
E                           https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues with
E                           information on how to reproduce this. (error:030000BE:digital envelope routines:EVP_CIPHER_CTX_copy:not able to copy ctx:crypto/evp/evp_enc.c:1792:)
```

This has been test with `46.0.7` but is likely a regression added by 98dfafeb8dcdf5e640c9612841f07da66586509b. The version 41.0.7 from the Red Hat package python3.12-cryptography does not exhibit this problem.

A possible workaround is to use `aesgcm = Cipher(algorithms.AES(key), modes.GCM(iv)).encryptor()` instead as that still works.

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @schwabe 2026-05-04T16:27:23Z:
After a bit of discussion in #pyca irc channel it looks like the main culprit is that `aead.rs`  uses LazyEvpCipherAead vs EvpCipherAead based on CRYPTOGRAPHY_OPENSSL_320_OR_GREATER but depending on the main OpenSSL version. So if a FIPS module uses a lower version (3.0.7 in this case) than the main OpenSSL version, it selects an implementation that only works with the default provider but not with the fips provider.
---
[c2] @alex 2026-05-04T22:11:56Z:
As discussed on IRC, I think this is a consequence of us using build-time feature detection and that being effectively inaccurate due to OpenSSL allowing (and RHEL choosing to) mixing-and-matching OpenSSL and provider versions.

This is one where if someone comes up with a PR that's appropriately maintainable, I'm happy to review and consider it, but I'm not going to do any work on this myself. And if it's not possible to fix in a reasonable way, that'll just be Yet Another Unfortunate Consequence of OpenSSL's unfortunate design choices: https://cryptography.io/en/latest/statements/state-of-openssl/
---
[c3] @alex 2026-05-05T11:36:50Z:
Additional note: we test against centos-stream 9 in CI, so it'd be interesting to understand why that's fine.
---
[c4] @schwabe 2026-05-05T12:23:51Z:
The reason is that Centos 9 stream does not ship with a _certified_  FIPS module but just with a "random" FIPS module that is built from the version as OpenSSL itself:

```
[14:22]{1}arne@centos9-fips:~% openssl list -providers
Providers:
  base
    name: OpenSSL Base Provider
    version: 3.5.5
    status: active
  default
    name: OpenSSL Default Provider
    version: 3.5.5
    status: active
  fips
    name: Red Hat Enterprise Linux OpenSSL FIPS Provider
    version: 3.5.5-ab02c3b56688c2b8
    status: active
```

vs

```
[14:23]arne@rhel9-fips:~% openssl list -providers
Providers:
  base
    name: OpenSSL Base Provider
    version: 3.5.1
    status: active
  default
    name: OpenSSL Default Provider
    version: 3.5.1
    status: active
  fips
    name: Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 - OpenSSL FIPS Provider
    version: 3.0.7-395c1a240fbfffd8
    status: active
```
---
[c5] @abbra 2026-05-06T14:48:50Z:
I added a fix that tries if the newer call works first time and then falls back to old if it doesn't. @schwabe can you try that in your environment?
---

title: illegal instruction on arm
need_summary: The crash is caused by Docker exposing incorrect ARM CPU features (SVE) leading to an illegal instruction in OpenSSL, as linked in Docker for Mac issue #7583, and can be mitigated by disabling SVE via kernel parameters (see VectorCamp issue #355).
security_topic: illegal instruction caused by SVE feature exposure in Docker on ARM
question_text: illegal instruction on arm
answer_text: I've managed to fix my issue by disabling sve on the kernel via a grub command line parameter. I also ensured I was fully updated on Debian (apt update/upgrade). Details of the command line change in case anyone needs it in the future is here - https://github.com/VectorCamp/vectorscan/issues/355.

[c13] @reaperhulk 2026-05-09T12:18:49Z:
Try upgrading parallels. The issue here was that docker had bugs in their docker desktop product which runs a VM and then executes docker containers inside that VM. Specifically their VM subsystem was reporting CPU capabilities that the underlying chip didn’t actually possess. With cryptography 47+ we now bundle OpenSSL 4, which had some new assembly optimizations which tried to take advantage of the reported features. Since they don’t exist this causes a crash.

[c19] @reaperhulk 2026-05-23T14:07:54Z:
Failing on the sigill with SVE means the virtual machine manager is exposing the wrong capabilities to the guest operating system. M4 and M5 do not have a complete SVE implementation in hardware. If you’re running a Linux VM and then docker inside that, Docker is not the issue here. The original filed issue was that docker desktop on Mac actually has its own Linux VM, and older versions had this VM bug. However, when you run docker inside a Linux VM yourself, it cannot cause this problem. Only the hypervisor/VMM can.
---
[c20] @RogerSelwyn 2026-05-23T14:52:50Z:
@reaperhulk thank you for the info. I’ll try using Parallels to see if that solves the problem. I also have an M1 Mini where I run my production Home Assistant so I can try standing up a container on there with Cryptography to see if that has the problem since you say it is M4/M5 with the issue. 

I’ll also have a go at reporting to VMWare/Broadcom, big corporation so no idea how quick any response will be. 
---
[c21] @RogerSelwyn 2026-05-23T15:14:17Z:
OK, I'm starting to understand more. M1 doesn't have sve features (sve2, svei18mm, svebf16) whilst my M4 does. Are you able to tell me what the feature flags should be on an M4/M5 or is it more complicated than that?
---
[c22] @reaperhulk 2026-05-23T15:23:21Z:
The VMM needs to be automatically identifying this. I do not know what the precise set should be offhand, no.
---
[c23] @RogerSelwyn 2026-05-23T15:24:36Z:
> The VMM needs to be automatically identifying this. I do not know what the precise set should be offhand, no.

Thanks
---
[c24] @RogerSelwyn 2026-05-23T16:06:40Z:
I've managed to fix my issue by disabling sve on the kernel via a grub command line parameter. I also ensured I was fully updated on Debian (apt update/upgrade).

Details of the command line change in case anyone needs it in the future is here - https://github.com/VectorCamp/vectorscan/issues/355. I'll still try to raise a case on VMWare.

comments.author: reaperhulk
comments.body: Try upgrading parallels. The issue here was that docker had bugs in their docker desktop product which runs a VM and then executes docker containers inside that VM. Specifically their VM subsystem was reporting CPU capabilities that the underlying chip didn’t actually possess. With cryptography 47+ we now bundle OpenSSL 4, which had some new assembly optimizations which tried to take advantage of the reported features. Since they don’t exist this causes a crash.

comments.author: reaperhulk
comments.body: Failing on the sigill with SVE means the virtual machine manager is exposing the wrong capabilities to the guest operating system. M4 and M5 do not have a complete SVE implementation in hardware. If you’re running a Linux VM and then docker inside that, Docker is not the issue here. The original filed issue was that docker desktop on Mac actually has its own Linux VM, and older versions had this VM bug. However, when you run docker inside a Linux VM yourself, it cannot cause this problem. Only the hypervisor/VMM can.

ISSUE #14690: Tracking: Post-quantum cryptography (ML-KEM / ML-DSA / SLH-DSA) support roadmap
Author: maddykws
Date: 2026-04-18T13:58:06Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
Hey all,

First — I know this library *implements* RSA and ECC. That's the point. 
This isn't a "you have vulnerabilities" issue. It's more of a "where are 
we on PQC support and can I help" issue.

Context: I've been building a scanner (QuantumMigrate) that audits 
codebases for quantum-vulnerable crypto usage. I ran it on this repo 
mostly out of curiosity, and it flagged 174 usages in src/ alone — which 
is completely expected given what this library does. But it made me 
wonder about the roadmap for NIST PQC support.

NIST finalized three standards in 2024:
- ML-KEM (FIPS 203) — key encapsulation, replaces RSA/DH/ECDH
- ML-DSA (FIPS 204) — signatures, replaces RSA/ECDSA/DSA  
- SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) — hash-based signatures, conservative backup

The deadline pressure is real. "Harvest now, decrypt later" means 
encrypted data being sent over TLS today is potentially being stockpiled. 
The sensitive stuff — healthcare records, financial transactions, anything 
with a long confidentiality window — is already at risk.

A few specific things I noticed in the source that seem worth discussing:

**ssh.py (22 hits)** — RSA and ECC key types for SSH. OpenSSH already 
merged experimental support for ML-KEM-768 in OpenSSH 9.0. Is there a 
plan to surface that here once it stabilises in the spec?

**_oid.py (lines 128-148)** — SHA1 and MD5 in the OID signature 
algorithm map. I understand these exist for parsing legacy certs, but 
is there appetite for a deprecation warning when they're used for 
*signing* (not just parsing)?

**ec.py / rsa.py** — Core implementations obviously stay, but are there 
plans to add ML-KEM and ML-DSA alongside them? OpenSSL 3.5 shipped 
post-quantum support in March 2026. Since cryptography wraps OpenSSL, 
I'd imagine this is closer than it looks.

I'm not expecting you to rip out RSA tomorrow. I'm genuinely asking 
whether there's an existing tracking issue I missed, whether there's a 
preferred way to contribute PQC primitives if OpenSSL exposes them, or 
whether this is something the maintainers have already scoped.

Happy to help however makes sense — testing, docs, whatever.

Thanks for maintaining one of the most important libraries in the Python 
ecosystem.

— scanned with https://github.com/maddykws/QuantumMigrate

Our next release will have ML-KEM and ML-DSA support, and there's a distinct issue for SLH-DSA: #14419.

I recognize your issue is attempting to be polite, but it appears you didn't make any effort to search the issue tracker for prior art here. Further, most of your analysis of "place to look in the codebase" are incredibly shallow, and don't add value.

title: Accessing unrelated extensions fails when BasicConstraints encodes default `ca:FALSE`
need_summary: The developer needed to know whether the library should accept certificates that explicitly encode the default ca:FALSE in BasicConstraints, and the maintainer answered that invalid DER is intentionally rejected, citing a design statement (see https://alexgaynor.net/2025/mar/25/postels-law-and-the-three-ring-circus/).
security_topic: strict DER validation causing unrelated extension access failure
question_text: Ideally, accessing an unrelated extension like SubjectAlternativeName should not fail due to a strict-DER violation in BasicConstraints.
answer_text:
This is an intentional design behavior.

In reverse order: We do not accept invalid DER, except in exceedingly rare cases. (See https://alexgaynor.net/2025/mar/25/postels-law-and-the-three-ring-circus/)
thread_text:
ISSUE #14592: Accessing unrelated extensions fails when BasicConstraints encodes default `ca:FALSE`
Author: st3fan
Date: 2026-04-07T00:22:15Z
Labels: waiting-on-reporter
State: closed

[c0]
# Accessing unrelated extensions fails when BasicConstraints encodes default `ca:FALSE`

## Versions

- Python: 3.13.5
- cryptography: 46.0.6
- OS: Debian Trixie (amd64)

## Description

When a certificate's `BasicConstraints` extension explicitly encodes `ca:FALSE` (the DER default value), the `cryptography` library raises a `ValueError` with `ParseError { kind: EncodedDefault }` when accessing **any** extension, not just `BasicConstraints`.

This means that calling `cert.extensions.get_extension_for_class(SubjectAlternativeName)` fails even though the SAN extension itself is perfectly valid. The error is thrown during iteration of the extensions list, making all extensions inaccessible.

The certificate is a real certificate observed in a Certificate Transparency log. OpenSSL parses it without errors and correctly shows `CA:FALSE` in the Basic Constraints and a valid SAN (`DNS:receptum-apteekkiverkko.maxx.fi, IP Address:83.150.105.126`).

While explicitly encoding the default value violates DER (the `ca` field defaults to `FALSE` per RFC 5280 and should be omitted), this encoding is common in the wild and is accepted by other implementations.

## Minimal PoC

```python
from cryptography import x509

der = open("entry_0046.der", "rb").read()
cert = x509.load_der_x509_certificate(der)

# This works fine:
print(cert.subject)
print(cert.issuer)

# This fails, even though SAN is valid:
san = cert.extensions.get_extension_for_class(x509.SubjectAlternativeName)
```

Output:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "poc.py", line 8, in <module>
    san = cert.extensions.get_extension_for_class(x509.SubjectAlternativeName)
          ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
  ...
ValueError: error parsing asn1 value: ParseError { kind: EncodedDefault, location: ["BasicConstraints::ca"] }
```

## OpenSSL output

OpenSSL parses the same certificate without issue:

```
$ openssl x509 -inform DER -in entry_0046.der -text -noout
Certificate:
    Data:
        Version: 3 (0x2)
        Serial Number:
            01:99:3d:78:70:fe:f2:ca:f0:9b:b6:c9:d1:78:28
        Signature Algorithm: sha512WithRSAEncryption
        Issuer: C=FI, O=Digi- ja vaestotietovirasto CA, OU=Sosiaali- ja terveydenhuollon palveluvarmenteet, CN=DVV Social Welfare and Healthcare Service Certificates - G3R
        Validity
            Not Before: Oct 22 21:00:00 2025 GMT
            Not After : Oct 22 20:59:59 2026 GMT
        Subject: C=FI, ST=FINLAND, L=Naantali, O=Naantalin 2. apteekki, serialNumber=1.2.246.553.1.853.13.0, CN=83.150.105.126
        X509v3 extensions:
            X509v3 Basic Constraints: critical
                CA:FALSE
            X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
                DNS:receptum-apteekkiverkko.maxx.fi, IP Address:83.150.105.126
```

(Full output omitted for brevity. The certificate is attached as `entry_0046.pem.txt`.)

## Root cause

The BasicConstraints extension contains `30 03 01 01 00` — a SEQUENCE with an explicit `BOOLEAN FALSE`. Per DER, the `ca` field defaults to `FALSE` and must be omitted when it has the default value. The Rust ASN.1 parser in `cryptography` strictly rejects this as `EncodedDefault`. Since extension parsing is all-or-nothing, this makes every extension on the certificate inaccessible.

## Expected behavior

Ideally, accessing an unrelated extension like `SubjectAlternativeName` should not fail due to a strict-DER violation in `BasicConstraints`. Possible approaches:

1. Parse extensions lazily so that accessing one extension doesn't require successfully parsing all others.
2. Accept the common DER violation of explicitly encoding default values in `BasicConstraints`.

[entry_0046.pem.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26522833/entry_0046.pem.txt)

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @alex 2026-04-07T00:37:46Z:
This is an intentional design behavior.

In reverse order: We do not accept invalid DER, except in exceedingly rare cases. (See https://alexgaynor.net/2025/mar/25/postels-law-and-the-three-ring-circus/)

As for the issue of unrelated extensions, the most recent time this was brought up was https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/13504#issuecomment-3368256526 (but I'm reasonably certain there's been other issues about this)


---
[c2] @st3fan 2026-04-07T00:53:25Z:
Thanks @alex - I think that is fair. Because this is so extremely rare (I parsed more than 100,000,000 certificates before this happened) I will use a fallback parser when this specific error happens. Thank you for the clear response.
---
[c3] @SillyZir 2026-04-10T11:14:43Z:
The extension iterator likely validates all extensions collectively; `ParseError { kind: EncodedDefault }` from `BasicConstraints` bubbles up on any access. Consider treating `EncodedDefault` as a recoverable warning in the Rust extension parser rather than a hard error.
---

thread_text:
ISSUE #14477: Fix for CVE-2026-26007 breaks ecc
Author: mdeslaur
Date: 2026-03-14T12:30:49Z
Labels: waiting-on-reporter
State: closed

[c0]
Hi,

We have gotten a report that the fix for CVE-2026-26007 included in 46.0.5 is breaking Ansible.

Ansible now returns the following error:
fatal: [localhost]: FAILED! => changed=false
msg: Your cryptography version does not support SECP384R1

A simple reproducer for this issue is:
```
import cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ec
ecclass = cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ec.__dict__.get('SECP384R1')
print(ecclass)
```

Downstream bug report for possibly more information:
https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/python-cryptography/+bug/2144373
(We had backported the security fix to our stable releases in Ubuntu, but the same issue is present in 46.0.5)

Thanks!

[c1] @alex 2026-03-14T12:33:35Z:
I assume this is an unexpeted consequene of our `deprecated` utility: https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/commit/0eebb9dbb6343d9bc1d91e5a2482ed4e054a6d8c#diff-42b5786fb7abc7aa972632f10f1a9e5e7fa2184943dda31d2671690d489c579cR461-R464

That said, accessing things via `__dict__` isn't really the correct way to get attributes from a module.

---
[c3] @alex 2026-03-14T12:48:11Z:

ISSUE #14334: 46.0.5: community.crypto reports "SECP256R1 not supported"
Author: paulhamby
Date: 2026-02-17T23:37:34Z
Labels: waiting-on-reporter
State: closed

[c0]
After upgrading from cryptography 46.0.4 to 46.0.5, the community.crypto Ansible collection fails when generating SECP256R1 ECC private keys, reporting "Your cryptography version does not support SECP256R1".

**Environment**
- cryptography version: 46.0.5 (broken), 46.0.4 (working)
- Python version: 3.13.11
- Platform: Fedora container (via Docker)
- community.crypto version: 2.26.6

**Reproduction Steps**

- Install cryptography 46.0.5
- Use community.crypto.openssl_privatekey with SECP256R1:

```
- name: Generate ECC private key
  community.crypto.openssl_privatekey:
    path: "/tmp/certificate.key"
    type: ECC
    curve: "secp256r1"
```

**Expected Behavior**

Key generation should succeed (as it does in 46.0.4)

**Actual Behavior**

```
fatal: [default -> localhost]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "Your cryptography version does not support SECP256R1"}
```

**Workaround**

Pinning to cryptography 46.0.4 resolves the issue:
```
pip install cryptography==46.0.4
```

title: Rust once_cell dependency has CVE-2019-16141 vulnerability

question_text: This issue is about to bump once_cell to latest version to close CVE-2019-16141 and keep once_cell up-to-date.
answer_text:
The version of once_cell specified in our Cargo.lock does not have that vulnerability (https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/main/Cargo.lock#L205-L209). I suspect, though I ahve not verified, that we have never dependened on a version with that vulnerability.

title: Extension criticality in EE certificates
need_summary: The developer needed to know whether 'N' in the Baseline Requirements means Criticality::NonCritical or Criticality::Agnostic, and the answer cites the CA/B Forum TLS Baseline Requirements and RFC 5280 stating it means Criticality::NonCritical.
security_topic: interpretation of baseline requirement criticality for X.509 extensions
question_text: It's a bit unclear to me if `N` in the BR should mean `Criticality::NonCritical` or `Criticality:Agnostic`? What's the interpretation of `pyca/cryptography`?
answer_text:
My interpretation of the CABF tables is that the symbols have the following meanings for criticality:

* `-` means "not applicable," usually because another requirement forbids the relevance of the criticality bit. For example, 7.1.2.7.6 says that Name Constrains MUST NOT appear in an EE cert, so criticality is `-`.
* `*` means agnostic. For example, 7.1.2.7.6 says that the SAN MUST appear, but can be either critical or non-critical.
* `Y` and `N` mean MUST and MUST NOT be critical, respectively.

So yeah, I believe `N` in the BRs should mean `Criticality::NonCritical`, and for the Subject Key Identifier in particular NOT RECOMMENDED doesn't have a bearing on the criticality constraint (we accept it either way, but we *don't* accept it as critical because that specific state is forbidden rather than NOT RECOMMENDED).
thread_text:
ISSUE #14173: Extension criticality in EE certificates
Author: TaaviE
Date: 2026-01-19T15:31:06Z
Labels: waiting-on-reporter, Stale
State: closed

[c0]
The current implementation in [`extensions.rs`](https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/main/src/rust/cryptography-x509-verification/src/policy/extension.rs#L118) seems to apply the BR a bit inconsistent. I personally stumbled upon it erroring when EKU was marked as critical, which is allowed by RFC 5280 but `N` in the BR and marked as `Criticality:NonCritical`. At the same time `subjectKeyIdentifier` is `N` (and `NOT RECOMMENDED`) but marked as `Criticality::Agnostic`.

It's a bit unclear to me if `N` in the BR should mean `Criticality::NonCritical` or `Criticality:Agnostic`? What's the interpretation of `pyca/cryptography`?

It seems more reasonable to be `Agnostic` of criticality if it's allowed by RFC 5280 (and has a purpose) and `NonCritical` when an extension has been widely considered non-critical. 

#### References

The tables in CA/B Forum TLS Server certificate BR currently specifies the following:

CA-Browser-Forum TLS BR 2.2.2:
> 7.1.2.7.6 Subscriber Certificate Extensions: 

| Extension | Presence | Critical | Description |
|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| authorityInformationAccess | MUST | N | See Section 7.1.2.7.7 |
| authorityKeyIdentifier | MUST | N | See Section 7.1.2.11.1 |
| certificatePolicies | MUST | N | See Section 7.1.2.7.9 |
| extKeyUsage | MUST | N | See Section 7.1.2.7.10 |
| subjectAltName | MUST | * | See Section 7.1.2.7.12 |
| nameConstraints | MUST NOT | ‐ |  - |
| keyUsage | SHOULD | Y |  See Section 7.1.2.7.11 |
| basicConstraints | MAY  | Y |  See Section 7.1.2.7.8 |
| crlDistributionPoints | * |  N |  See Section 7.1.2.11.2 |
| Signed Certificate Timestamp List | MAY  | N |  See Section 7.1.2.11.3 |
| subjectKeyIdentifier | NOT RECOMMENDED | N |  See Section 7.1.2.11.4 |
| Any other extension | NOT RECOMMENDED | ‐ |  See Section 7.1.2.11.5 |

CA-Browser-Forum TLS BR 2.2.2:
> 7.1.2 Certificate Content and Extensions
```
If the CA asserts compliance with these Baseline Requirements, all certificates that it issues MUST
comply with one of the following certificate profiles, which incorporate, and are derived from RFC
5280.
```

RFC 5280:
```
   If a CA includes extended key usages to satisfy such applications,
   but does not wish to restrict usages of the key, the CA can include
   the special KeyPurposeId anyExtendedKeyUsage in addition to the
   particular key purposes required by the applications.  Conforming CAs
   SHOULD NOT mark this extension as critical if the anyExtendedKeyUsage
   KeyPurposeId is present.  Applications that require the presence of a
   particular purpose MAY reject certificates that include the
   anyExtendedKeyUsage OID but not the particular OID expected for the
   application.
```

extensions.rs:
```rust
            subject_key_identifier: ExtensionValidator::maybe_present(
                SUBJECT_KEY_IDENTIFIER_OID,
                Criticality::Agnostic,
                None,
            ),
[...]
            // CA/B: 7.1.2.7.10: Subscriber Certificate Extended Key Usage
            // NOTE: CABF requires EKUs in EE certs, while RFC 5280 does not.
            extended_key_usage: ExtensionValidator::maybe_present(
                EXTENDED_KEY_USAGE_OID,
                Criticality::NonCritical,
                Some(Arc::new(ee::extended_key_usage)),
            ),
```

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @woodruffw 2026-01-19T15:56:23Z:
> It's a bit unclear to me if `N` in the BR should mean `Criticality::NonCritical` or `Criticality:Agnostic`? What's the interpretation of `pyca/cryptography`?

My interpretation of the CABF tables is that the symbols have the following meanings for criticality:

* `-` means "not applicable," usually because another requirement forbids the relevance of the criticality bit. For example, 7.1.2.7.6 says that Name Constrains MUST NOT appear in an EE cert, so criticality is `-`.
* `*` means agnostic. For example, 7.1.2.7.6 says that the SAN MUST appear, but can be either critical or non-critical.
* `Y` and `N` mean MUST and MUST NOT be critical, respectively.

So yeah, I believe `N` in the BRs should mean `Criticality::NonCritical`, and for the Subject Key Identifier in particular NOT RECOMMENDED doesn't have a bearing on the criticality constraint (we accept it either way, but we *don't* accept it as critical because that specific state is forbidden rather than NOT RECOMMENDED).
---
[c2] @woodruffw 2026-01-19T15:57:39Z:
With that said, I think PyCA Cryptography's general position with respect to BR conformance is that the validator should reflect real-world (i.e. Web PKI) behavior. Are you aware of publicly issued EEs that exhibit a critical SKI, or is this something you've hit on non-Web PKI issuances?
---
[c3] @TaaviE 2026-01-19T16:27:14Z:
> So yeah, I believe N in the BRs should mean Criticality::NonCritical, and for the Subject Key Identifier in particular NOT RECOMMENDED doesn't have a bearing on the criticality constraint (we accept it either way, but we don't accept it as critical because that specific state is forbidden rather than NOT RECOMMENDED).

SKI is `Agnostic` right now though? Is it actually not accepted as critical?

>  Are you aware of publicly issued EEs that exhibit a critical SKI, or is this something you've hit on non-Web PKI issuances?

Neither, nor have I searched for Web PKI issuances. I encountered a critical EKU in non-Web PKI and started looking into why it was being restricted.

Right now it seems that:
* SKI is `Agnostic` when it should be `NonCritical`
* KU is `Agnostic` when it should be `Critical`
* BC is `Agnostic` when it should be `Critical`

(and EKU is `NonCritical` when `Agnostic` would make a bit more sense to require usage enforcement)

I can make a PR to align the checks with the BR.
---
[c4] @alex 2026-01-19T16:30:02Z:
I'm almost positive that in all cases we are _less_ strict than the BRs, it's because there is no security value in it and there was enough ecosystem breakage that it didn't make sense to strictly enforce. If there are cases we're more strict than the specs we should probably fix that!
---
[c5] @woodruffw 2026-01-19T16:33:52Z:
Oh, my bad -- I thought you were saying that we weren't already agnostic. I agree that's a bit inconsistent at the moment.

I'm kind of surprised we don't have an x509-limbo testcase for this 🙂 -- that would be a good guidepost for whether we can/should restrict criticality. 
---
[c6] @TaaviE 2026-01-20T11:37:09Z:
Should I make a PR to change EKU to `Agnostic` to match the enforcement of other extensions' criticality? Or do you wish to first create a test-case in `x509-limbo` to figure out which extensions' criticality can be enforced according to the BR?

Maybe it would be better to follow the BR unless specifically overridden by the user (or code using the crate/library)? That way any deviations from BR would be explicit.
---
[c7] @alex 2026-01-20T12:28:35Z:
Unless there's a pressing reason, our preference is to match the BRs. It looks like we already have a testcase for this: https://x509-limbo.com/testcases/webpki/#webpkiekuee-critical-eku

(Though it shows as skipped, which is surprising to me.)
---
[c8] @woodruffw 2026-01-20T12:56:14Z:
> It looks like we already have a testcase for this

That one is for critical EKU in EEs, not critical SKI. I think we could indeed use a new limbo testcase for this!

> Though it shows as skipped, which is surprising to me.

I don't remember exactly, but I _think_ we skipped some of these because none of the other validators checked them. So the idea was that the breakage risk was too high, although now that there's a custom policy API that's probably moot.
---
[c9] @github-actions 2026-01-24T00:00:15Z:
This issue has been waiting for a reporter response for 3 days. It will be auto-closed if no activity occurs in the next 5 days.
---
[c10] @github-actions 2026-01-29T00:00:37Z:
This issue has not received a reporter response and has been auto-closed. If the issue is still relevant please leave a comment and we can reopen it.
---
[c11] @alex 2026-01-29T12:28:15Z:
I can re-open, but unless I'm confused, it's not clear there's any action to take here: https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/14173#issuecomment-3772648357
---
[c12] @TaaviE 2026-01-29T16:11:49Z:
Well, the policy enforcement should be based on something (like WebPKI observations) or aligned to the BR. It's up to you as maintainers to decide which approach should be taken. Whichever way is taken in the future, it's still inconsistent right now and the issue itself should remain open.
---
[c13] @alex 2026-01-29T16:17:18Z:
Our policy is that we align to BRs or RFC5280, as appropriate, but we make things laxer when it's either required for interoperability in practice or is a property no other validators enforce.

In this case, we're matching the BRs behavior, and I don't think we've really established that there's an interop risk, hence there being no change to make here.
---
[c14] @TaaviE 2026-01-30T10:28:20Z:
> In this case, we're matching the BRs behavior

To match the BR the following changes should be made:

* SKI is `Agnostic` -> should be `NonCritical`
* KU is `Agnostic` -> should be `Critical`
* BC is `Agnostic` -> should be `Critical`


---
[c15] @alex 2026-01-30T12:11:24Z:
Sorry, I feel like we're talking with circles: places where we are laxer than the BRs are generally intentional, and reflect things that:

> it's either required for interoperability in practice or is a property no other validators enforce.


---
[c16] @TaaviE 2026-01-30T12:36:09Z:
Adding documentation that "this is done because others do it", "this is required for interop" would also address the core of this issue. Almost my entire point is that it doesn't match the RFC nor the BR and it's not written anywhere why that is the case.
---

thread_text:
ISSUE #14073: Add HPKE support
Author: alex
Date: 2025-12-30T17:02:54Z
Labels: api design, good first issue
State: closed

[c0]
We've gotten some feedback that it'd be valuable for us to add HPKE support.

TODO:

- [x] Review RFC, decide what subset (if any) we think makes sense to implemen
- [ ] Design an API
  - [ ] Is this sufficiently misuse resistant that it could be considered a recipe (i.e., not hazmat)?
- [x] Gather test vectors/KATs
- [ ] Implement (including tests + docs)


--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @alex 2025-12-30T17:11:51Z:
Inspiration on scope + API:

- https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/cloudflare/circl/hpke
- https://github.com/ctz/hpke-py/
- https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/internal/hpke
- https://docs.rs/hpke/latest/hpke/

---
[c2] @SalusaSecondus 2025-12-30T20:55:36Z:
My own two cents:

1. 1 shot base mode is definitely safe enough to expose as a recipe. (This is especially true if it can return a single "ciphertext" consisting of both the encapsulated key and the ciphertext.)
2. Base mode (in general) is *probably* safe enough to expose as a recipe.
3. As useful as I personally find it, the Auth modes may not be worth building in :-(
4. PSK modes, while safe, might be better in hazmat simply because reasoning about them can be complicated.
5. Exported secrets is a critical feature (but very possibly hazmat)
---
[c3] @alex 2025-12-30T21:02:25Z:
Thank you! If we think its right that different modes should live in different layers, that has some (fiddly!) implications for our API design.
---
[c4] @SalusaSecondus 2025-12-30T23:01:14Z:
Something I've built into my (non-public, unfortunately) implementations of HPKE is a unified 1-shot interface which I think is the ideal one to expose as non-hazmat. While the specification [does describe it](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9180.html#section-6), the below combines the return values into one which I think is better for the average user. (If people care about compatibility with other implementations, they can simply split off the constant-length prefix from their ciphertexts here.)

(Doing Java for API definition because I'm much better at it than Python. Sorry.)

```java
enum HpkeKem{};
enum HpkeKdf{};
enum HpkeAead{};

// Returns encapsulated key + ciphertext
byte[] oneShotHpkeSeal(
    HpkeKem kem,
    HpkeKdf kdf,
    HpkeAead aead,
    byte[] recipientPublicKey,
    byte[] info,
    byte[] aad,
    byte[] plaintext);

byte[] oneShotHpkeOpen(
    HpkeKem kem,
    HpkeKdf kdf,
    HpkeAead aead,
    byte[] recipientPrivateKey,
    byte[] info,
    byte[] aad,
    byte[] ciphertext);
```

So, with the above in normal and all detailed implementations in hazmat, I think we've a safe interface.
---
[c5] @FiloSottile 2025-12-31T21:57:19Z:
We are shipping a public API in Go 1.26, so I have _thoughts_ :)

https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/hpke@go1.26rc1

We shipped only base mode, not PSK-authenticated (which requires high-entropy secrets and feels like it will be misused with passwords) nor KEM-authenticated which is being removed in -bis and is not compatible with PQ.

We actually shipped the PQ KEMs and SHAKE KDF, even if they are drafts. We got informal commitments the wire encoding won't change (except for security issues ofc) and it feels wrong to ship without PQ at this point.

You might find this summary useful since the PQ KEMs are defined over four different documents: [filippo.io/hpke-pq](https://filippo.io/hpke-pq)

I played a lot with the API, you can see iterations and rationales at golang/go#75300.

In short, public functions return AED/KDF/KEM interface types with ID methods. The KEMs are interfaces with GenerateKey/NewPublicKey/NewPrivateKey/DeriveKeyPair methods. NewSender takes PublicKey + KDF + AEAD, and returns a type that can do Seal and Export. NewRecipient takes encapsulated key + PrivateKey + KDF + AEAD, and returns a type that can do Open and Export.

We have one-shot Open and Seal which take info BUT NOT aad (since they are redundant and the RFC recommends picking info for one-shot). They return/take a single `enc || ciphertext` slice.

The named public functions encourage picking one KEM, one KDF, one AEAD, instead of supporting them all.

Something I've built into my (non-public, unfortunately) implementations of HPKE is a unified 1-shot interface which I think is the ideal one to expose as non-hazmat. While the specification [does describe it](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9180.html#section-6), the below combines the return values into one which I think is better for the average user. (If people care about compatibility with other implementations, they can simply split off the constant-length prefix from their ciphertexts here.)

(Doing Java for API definition because I'm much better at it than Python. Sorry.)

```java
enum HpkeKem{};
enum HpkeKdf{};
enum HpkeAead{};

// Returns encapsulated key + ciphertext
byte[] oneShotHpkeSeal(
    HpkeKem kem,
    HpkeKdf kdf,
    HpkeAead aead,
    byte[] recipientPublicKey,
    byte[] info,
    byte[] aad,
    byte[] plaintext);

byte[] oneShotHpkeOpen(
    HpkeKem kem,
    HpkeKdf kdf,
    HpkeAead aead,
    byte[] recipientPrivateKey,
    byte[] info,
    byte[] aad,
    byte[] ciphertext);
```

So, with the above in normal and all detailed implementations in hazmat, I think we've a safe interface.

comments.author: FiloSottile
comments.body:
We are shipping a public API in Go 1.26, so I have _thoughts_ :)

https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/hpke@go1.26rc1

We shipped only base mode, not PSK-authenticated (which requires high-entropy secrets and feels like it will be misused with passwords) nor KEM-authenticated which is being removed in -bis and is not compatible with PQ.

We actually shipped the PQ KEMs and SHAKE KDF, even if they are drafts. We got informal commitments the wire encoding won't change (except for security issues ofc) and it feels wrong to ship without PQ at this point.

You might find this summary useful since the PQ KEMs are defined over four different documents: [filippo.io/hpke-pq](https://filippo.io/hpke-pq)

I played a lot with the API, you can see iterations and rationales at golang/go#75300.

In short, public functions return AED/KDF/KEM interface types with ID methods. The KEMs are interfaces with GenerateKey/NewPublicKey/NewPrivateKey/DeriveKeyPair methods. NewSender takes PublicKey + KDF + AEAD, and returns a type that can do Seal and Export. NewRecipient takes encapsulated key + PrivateKey + KDF + AEAD, and returns a type that can do Open and Export.

We have one-shot Open and Seal which take info BUT NOT aad (since they are redundant and the RFC recommends picking info for one-shot). They return/take a single `enc || ciphertext` slice.

The named public functions encourage picking one KEM, one KDF, one AEAD, instead of supporting them all.

The RFC has test vectors, and https://github.com/hpkewg/hpke-pq/blob/main/test-vectors.json are the vectors for the PQ KEMs and SHAKE KDF suites.

Maybe the difference between hazmat and recipe is that the recipe picks the AEAD, KDF, and PQ KEM for the user.

- All 3 KDFs (HKDF-SHA256/384/512)
- 3 AEADs (AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305)
- Secret export via `context.export()`
- RFC 9180 A.1.1 test vectors

A few questions before I open the PR:

1. **Naming**: You mentioned not loving `sender`/`recipient` or `seal`/`open`. Any preferred alternatives? Some options:
   - `encryptor`/`decryptor` with `encrypt`/`decrypt`?
   - `encap`/`decap` (closer to RFC terminology)?

2. **Return format**: Should `seal()` return just the ciphertext (current), or concatenate `enc + ciphertext` like Go does for single-shot use?

3. **Parameter order**: I went with `Suite(AEAD, KEM, KDF)` - is that the order you prefer, or should it match RFC order (KEM, KDF, AEAD)?

Happy to adjust before submitting!

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
@reaperhulk let me know how you feel about these:

1. Naming: I think maybe let's just use encrypt/decrypt? That's what we use for our AEAD interfaces.
2. `enc || ciphertext` in line with Go seems good to me
3. Go matches the RFC (though it takes a key type, rather than an KEM enum) -- unless there's a conflicting argument, let's match that.
4. Let's drop export

comments.author: reaperhulk
comments.body:
Most implementations appear to use open/seal, which is interesting. If we want encrypt/decrypt we will be consistent with ourselves and inconsistent with the wider ecosystem, but I suppose we could just alias to give open/seal in the future if needed.

I think, absent aliasing, I'd prefer encrypt/decrypt for internal consistency and general clarity of purpose.

No objections on 2-4.

comments.author: bifurcation
comments.body:
> Most implementations appear to use open/seal, which is interesting.

I suspect that this is just an artifact of the language in RFC 9180.

comments.author: alex
comments.body: It's also pretty standard for AEADs in general IMO. I think we're a bit contrarian in not liking it.

comments.author: FiloSottile
comments.body:
[ I wrote a long version of this comment and I think GitHub lost it?! Sorry for the briefness of the redo. ]

The one in https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/14073#issuecomment-3726654797 looks like a multi-step API, in which case seal should return just the ciphertext, just like open does not take enc. If you make a single-step API, then it should be suite.open / suite.seal without the intermediate sender/recipient.

Note that if you don't make key objects you preclude doing per-key precomputations.

Naming the DHKEMs DHKEM_X25519_HKDF_SHA256 is IMHO humoring the IETF too far. There will never be a DHKEM_X25519_SOMETHING_ELSE and the double KDF is confusing.

I think both open/seal and decrypt/encrypt are fine. I don't like sender/recipient but they are in the RFC and I don't have better suggestions.

> [@FiloSottile](https://github.com/FiloSottile) is there a reason you went with `DHKEM(ecdh.Curve)` rather than having 4 separate functions each with their own KEM?

Not a strong one, I like the ecdh closed interface and explicit dependencies.

Not sure if it's too late, but I wouldn't include both info and aad in a one-shot API, there is no point in using both. AAD is only separate because in the multi-message API it's per-message. IIRC the RFC discourages exposing both from one-shot APIs, too.

Go's one-shot API only takes info.

title: On some plateforms, DHParameterNumbers performance is 100x slower
need_summary: The slowdown is caused by the DH_check security validation and has been fixed by skipping well‑known parameters in LibreSSL 4.3.0 (see commit 9ac14cf7a1b28db2437e849540c0abe6a436a03d).
security_topic: DH parameter validation performance issue in LibreSSL
question_text: What do you think could be the issue here ? Am I doing something wrong ?
answer_text: Now landed, the main bit is here: https://github.com/openbsd/src/commit/9ac14cf7a1b28db2437e849540c0abe6a436a03d and a follow-on added RFC 7919 primes. So this should no longer be a problem with LibreSSL 4.3.0 and later.
thread_text:
ISSUE #14048: On some plateforms, DHParameterNumbers performance is 100x slower
Author: gpotter2
Date: 2025-12-23T01:37:27Z
Labels: waiting-on-reporter
State: closed

[c0]
Hi everyone !

First of all, merry Christmas !

I have been troubleshooting some issues with scapy being super slow to load one some plateforms, and have cornered the problem to a very big performance difference when running `DHParameterNumbers.parameters()` on some plateforms. My setups are sadly very different, and this will likely need further troubleshooting to precisely identify what's wrong.

Here's the code to reproduce:
```python
from cryptography.hazmat.backends import default_backend
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.dh import DHParameterNumbers

# modp8192 parameters
# https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3526 sect 7
g = 2
m = 

pn = DHParameterNumbers(m, g)
params = pn.parameters(default_backend())
```

| OS|  Flavor |  Python |  Time to run |
|---|---|---|---|
|Debian 13 | OpenSSL 3.5.1 (FIPS: False, Legacy: True) |  3.13.5 |  0m0.086s real 0m0.069s user     0m0.017s system |
|OpenBSD 78 |  LibreSSL 4.2.0 (FIPS: False, Legacy: False) |  3.12.11 |  **1m03.48s** real     **1m03.32s** user 0m00.08s system |

(both are running in Hyper-V virtual machines. It would be unfair to say those stats are 1-to-1 comparable, but it feels like a very high difference.)

What do you think could be the issue here ? Am I doing something wrong ?

Thanks a lot for the help and happy holidays !

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @alex 2025-12-23T01:40:46Z:
I believe its a known issue that LibreSSL performance with DH is quite slow: https://marc.info/?l=libressl&m=173846028619304&w=2
---
[c2] @gpotter2 2025-12-23T01:44:04Z:
This looks precisely like the issue !
Thanks for the note. To be fair, for well-known parameters (here modp8192), I would expect LibreSSL to somehow already know this is pretty safe (e.g. have a list of available parameters somewhere).


This isn't really a cryptography issue. If this is tracked elsewhere, feel free to close.

Thanks again for the help
---
[c3] @alex 2025-12-23T01:53:58Z:
I don't think the libressl folks have a bug tracker, so that thread is the closest it comes to being tracked anywhere. But given this isn't a cryptography bug and there's not really anything we can do to mitigate it, I'm going to close.
---
[c4] @botovq 2026-01-06T16:38:12Z:
If we really must, we can add shortcuts for the well-known domain-parameters to LibreSSL and cut down the cost of `DH_check()`, but I don't really understand why cryptography ends up calling `DH_check()` on well-known parameters in the first place.

Also, why is this done every time scapy starts up? My understanding is that `DH_check()` is intended for adversarial keys.

> I don't think the libressl folks have a bug tracker, so that thread is the closest it comes to being tracked anywhere. But given this isn't a cryptography bug and there's not really anything we can do to mitigate it, I'm going to close.

We monitor https://github.com/libressl/portable
---
[c5] @alex 2026-01-06T17:04:46Z:
Someone would have to trace through our code to remember which code path is calling `DH_check`, and whether its explicit in our code or comes via some other OpenSSL API. But fundamentally its' because we have no idea if a key is trusted or not :-) (And also OpenSSL is terribly unclear about when bad parameters can lead to UB vs. just leading to stupid crypto.)

If people want an opt-out, for RSA we added an `unsafe_skip_rsa_key_validation` flag and I suppose we could do the same for DH.
---
[c6] @botovq 2026-01-06T18:24:30Z:
Thanks. I think it always ends up being this call:

https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/5a23c88ece74c4a5f1ca46d40b6e987ca9a2f7b2/src/rust/src/backend/dh.rs#L121-L123

Be that as it may, there's now two python projects that were hurt by this. I guess I need to fix this... Sigh. It's 2026 and I still need to deal with DH... :)
---
[c7] @alex 2026-01-06T18:27:52Z:
Yes, that's the one place we call it explicitly -- this path isn't touched on PEM/DER parsing though. (Kind of sus)

FWIW every time I think about this I just want to delete FFDH entirely... alas...

---
[c8] @botovq 2026-01-06T18:35:07Z:
The domain parameters are instatiated via `DHParameterNumbers` or similar from constants stored in Scapy's python code itself, for example:

https://github.com/secdev/scapy/blob/40fc5ecf9e69e9bd76664d63ae133d4973fcf81b/scapy/layers/tls/crypto/groups.py#L49-L56
---
[c9] @reaperhulk 2026-01-06T18:39:46Z:
Hmm, if these were converted to PEM parameters and loaded via `load_pem_parameters` it would possibly remove the `DH_check` unless there's another one buried more deeply inside the functions we call during loading.
---
[c10] @alex 2026-01-06T19:16:46Z:
I don't think there is (arguably this is dumb, there's no valid reason there should be different checks for one vs the other)
---
[c11] @botovq 2026-01-06T19:20:13Z:
Neither LibreSSL nor modern OpenSSL call `DH_check()` internally. OpenSSL deprecated `DH_check()`, probably for the wrong reason, namely that it is using a "legacy primitive", not because it's a DoS vector (EVP_PKEY_check still is).
---
[c12] @botovq 2026-01-06T19:33:52Z:
Anyway. I'll see if I can get approval for landing code that skips the well-known parameters (I have a working diff). The annoying bit is that we don't have the RFC 7919 parameters because, well, why would we?

This should help pyca/cryptography that currently skips some tests for us because of this and the interactive use of Scapy 2.7.0 seems fine with my patch.

Thanks for the input so far!

Cc @sthen

title: `Name.rfc4514_string` emits non-parseable output for trailing spaces
need_summary: The developer needed to know if the double‑backslash escape for trailing spaces in Name.rfc4514_string() poses a security risk, and the answer cites RFC 4514 (which requires a single backslash) as the authoritative source confirming the serialization is non‑compliant.
security_topic: serialization bug causing non‑compliant DN encoding
question_text: I want to clarify, do you believe this is an issue with `rfc4514_string` or `from_rfc4514_string`?
answer_text:
Thanks for taking a look. I think the problem is on the serialization side.
If you run the repro and inspect the actual characters that `rfc4514_string()` returns, you’ll see there are two backslashes:
```python
from cryptography.x509 import Name
from cryptography.x509.name import NameAttribute
from cryptography.x509.oid import NameOID

name = Name([NameAttribute(NameOID.ORGANIZATION_NAME, " ")])
s = name.rfc4514_string()

print(s)                   # shows `O=\\ ` because Python escapes backslashes
print(list(s))             # ['O', '=', '\\', '\\', ' ']  ← two backslashes
print([ord(c) for c in s]) # […, 92, 92, 32]
```
RFC 4514 says a trailing space must be encoded as one backslash followed by a space. We’re emitting two backslashes plus space, which is not a valid escape sequence, so `from_rfc4514_string()` quite rightly rejects it. In other words, the parse failure is a consequence of `rfc4514_string()` producing non‑compliant output in this edge case.
thread_text:
ISSUE #13843: `Name.rfc4514_string` emits non-parseable output for trailing spaces
Author: T90REAL
Date: 2025-11-09T14:42:31Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
When an attribute value ends with a space, `Name.rfc4514_string()` escapes it incorrectly. The serializer outputs a string that `Name.from_rfc4514_string()` cannot parse, so the round-trip guarantee is broken.

```python
from cryptography.x509 import Name
from cryptography.x509.name import NameAttribute
from cryptography.x509.oid import NameOID

name = Name([NameAttribute(NameOID.COMMON_NAME, "0"),
             NameAttribute(NameOID.ORGANIZATION_NAME, " ")])
s = name.rfc4514_string()          # yields "CN=0,O=\\ "
Name.from_rfc4514_string(s)        # raises ValueError
```

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/data/src/test.py", line 8, in <module>
    Name.from_rfc4514_string(s)        # raises ValueError
    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/py312/lib/python3.12/site-packages/cryptography/x509/name.py", line 316, in from_rfc4514_string
    return _RFC4514NameParser(data, attr_name_overrides or {}).parse()
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/py312/lib/python3.12/site-packages/cryptography/x509/name.py", line 442, in parse
    self._read_char(",")
  File "/home/py312/lib/python3.12/site-packages/cryptography/x509/name.py", line 415, in _read_char
    raise ValueError
ValueError
```

FC 4514 requires trailing spaces to be escaped as `\` . Here I emit `\` (two backslashes plus space), which the parser rejects. 
Although it  is uncommon that the organization's name is just a space, any application relying on round-tripping—certificate tooling, directory synchronization, or sanitation of existing DNs with trailing spaces will hit this failure. A crafted DN from untrusted input could also trigger unexpected crashes.

## Versions tested on:
46.0.3

## Operating systems tested on:
Linux

```
  File "/home/py312/lib/python3.12/site-packages/cryptography/x509/name.py", line 316, in from_rfc4514_string
    return _RFC4514NameParser(data, attr_name_overrides or {}).parse()

  File "/home/py312/lib/python3.12/site-packages/cryptography/x509/name.py", line 442, in parse

  File "/home/py312/lib/python3.12/site-packages/cryptography/x509/name.py", line 415, in _read_char
    raise ValueError
```

FC 4514 requires trailing spaces to be escaped as `\` . Here I emit `\` (two backslashes plus space), which the parser rejects.

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
I want to clarify, do you believe this is an issue with `rfc4514_string` or `from_rfc4514_string`?

You say:
> When an attribute value ends with a space, Name.rfc4514_string() escapes it incorrectly.

However, you also say:
> RFC 4514 requires trailing spaces to be escaped as `\`

Which is what it seems to be doing.

Therefore, it looks to me like the issue is that we don't parse it, not that what we generate is invalid.

comments.author: T90REAL
comments.body:
Thanks for taking a look. I think the problem is on the serialization side.
If you run the repro and inspect the actual characters that `rfc4514_string()` returns, you’ll see there are two backslashes:
```python
from cryptography.x509 import Name
from cryptography.x509.name import NameAttribute
from cryptography.x509.oid import NameOID

name = Name([NameAttribute(NameOID.ORGANIZATION_NAME, " ")])
s = name.rfc4514_string()

print(s)                   # shows `O=\\ ` because Python escapes backslashes
print(list(s))             # ['O', '=', '\\', '\\', ' ']  ← two backslashes
print([ord(c) for c in s]) # […, 92, 92, 32]
```
RFC 4514 says a trailing space must be encoded as one backslash followed by a space. We’re emitting two backslashes plus space, which is not a valid escape sequence, so `from_rfc4514_string()` quite rightly rejects it. In other words, the parse failure is a consequence of `rfc4514_string()` producing non‑compliant output in this edge case.

title: key_size and group_order don't match for some obscure EC curves
need_summary: The developer needed to know why `key_size` and `group_order` differ for some EC curves, and the issue was resolved in PR #13750 (https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/pull/13750).
security_topic: EC curve key_size attribute mismatch with group order
question_text:
@hannob and I were talking about EC private key sizes, and he noticed that the `key_size` value in some of cryptography's `EllipticCurve` objects don't match the generated keys. They seem to be reporting the size of the field, but the docs say:

> Size (in bits) of a secret scalar for the curve (as generated by generate_private_key()).

That suggests that it should be the group order. Here's a little script that flags curves whose `group_order` and `key_size` fields don't match.

```
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import ec

curves = [
    ec.SECP256R1,
    ec.SECP384R1,
    ec.SECP521R1,
    ec.SECP224R1,
    ec.SECP192R1,
    ec.SECP256K1,
    ec.BrainpoolP256R1,
    ec.BrainpoolP384R1,
    ec.BrainpoolP512R1,
    ec.SECT571K1,
    ec.SECT409K1,
    ec.SECT283K1,
    ec.SECT233K1,
    ec.SECT163K1,
    ec.SECT571R1,
    ec.SECT409R1,
    ec.SECT283R1,
    ec.SECT233R1,
    ec.SECT163R2,
]

for curve in curves:
    # These should be equal. According to the docs, key_size is:
    # > Size (in bits) of a secret scalar for the curve (as generated
    # > by generate_private_key()).
    if curve.key_size != curve.group_order.bit_length():
        print(f"{curve.name} MISMATCH: key_size = {curve.key_size}; group_order.bit_length() = {curve.group_order.bit_length()}")

    # Confirm curve.group_order is indeed how private keys are generated.
    for _ in range(100):
        key = ec.generate_private_key(curve())
        assert key.private_numbers().private_value < curve.group_order

$ python3 curve_sizes.py 
sect571k1 MISMATCH: key_size = 571; group_order.bit_length() = 570
sect409k1 MISMATCH: key_size = 409; group_order.bit_length() = 407
sect283k1 MISMATCH: key_size = 283; group_order.bit_length() = 281
sect233k1 MISMATCH: key_size = 233; group_order.bit_length() = 232
sect283r1 MISMATCH: key_size = 283; group_order.bit_length() = 282
```
answer_text:
As the values are just hardcoded numbers in `ec.py`, a fix is easy.
Pull request: https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/pull/13750

title: Problem with an EC private key and load_der_private_key()
need_summary: The developer needed to know why certain DER-encoded private keys fail to load in version 45.0.0, and the answer explained that the keys use a PrivateKeyInfo version v2 which is invalid per RFC 5958.
security_topic: private key parsing failure due to invalid PrivateKeyInfo version
question_text: I have discovered a case where a private key was loaded correctly in version 44.0.3, and is no more in version 45.0.0. After analysing the key, it is a bit weird, with some supplemental useless "padding" bytes at the end... the key cannot be decoded with load_der_private_key() in version 45.0.0.
answer_text: These keys appear to have specified a PrivateKeyInfo version of v2 (integer value 1), which is invalid because that should only be set to v2 when a public key is present per RFC 5958.

```
cryptography.hazmat.primitives.serialization import load_der_private_key

der_key = bytes.fromhex("3041020100301306072a8648ce3d020106082a8648ce3d0301070427302502010104201445af4b5ea31dfc2043e41b527a78b0feed297bd367ff92920e80efc910eba8")

# bad key for version 45.0.0 and beyond
der_key = bytes.fromhex("3041020100301306072a8648ce3d020106082a8648ce3d0301070427302502010104201445af4b5ea31dfc2043e41b527a78b0feed297bd367ff92920e80efc910eba800000000000000000000000000")
print(der_key.hex())
try:
    key = load_der_private_key(der_key, password=None)
    print("the key is decoded")
except:
```

title: Possible incompatibility with OpenSSL FIPS mode
need_summary: The failure of RS256 verification in FIPS mode is due to a mismatch between the cryptography wheel’s statically linked OpenSSL and the FIPS provider; building cryptography from source against the same OpenSSL (see the CI run https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/actions/runs/17869821561/job/50820889775 and the compare branch https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/compare/experiment) resolves it.
security_topic: RS256 verification failure in FIPS mode
question_text: I'm reporting here because I couldn't find another API in cryptography for verifying an RSA signature.
answer_text:
I was able to replicate using your instructions, but when putting that into CI (https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/compare/experiment?expand=1) it passes on a FIPS build (https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/actions/runs/17869821561/job/50820889775).

It's possible this is due to some weirdness with the mismatch between the statically linked 3.5.3 in our wheel and the 3.1.2 FIPS provider being dynamically loaded. Officially that is allowed, but OpenSSL doesn't really test it well. What happens if you build everything yourself? To do so you'll need rustc, python-dev, and to compile with `OPENSSL_DIR=/path/to/custom/openssl pip install --no-binary cryptography cryptography`. Note that if you attempt to simply install into `/usr/local` you will likely run into symbol issues between Python (compiled with system OpenSSL) and cryptography, so I strongly recommend picking an alternate path.

ISSUE #13475: Possible incompatibility with OpenSSL FIPS mode
Author: cjpatton
Date: 2025-09-19T20:28:23Z
Labels: waiting-on-reporter, Stale
State: closed

[c0]
I have an application in scope of FIPS that needs to validate JWT tokens of type `RS256`. My best guess is that the `jwt` is trying to use a low level API that OpenSSL disables when running in FIPS mode. I'm reporting here because I couldn't find another API in `cryptography` for verifying an RSA signature.

`RS256` is RSA with PKCS#1 v1.5 padding and SHA256. I believe this should be FIPS compliant --- the public key in the test below has a 4096-bit modulus. The test also fails with `PS256`, which is RSA-PSS.

I'm on ARM64 and am building the OpenSSL 3.1.2 FIPS module. My backend is:
```
(.venv) root@4ea79d5dcc51:/w# OPENSSL_CONF=fips.cnf python
Python 3.13.5 (main, Jun 25 2025, 18:55:22) [GCC 14.2.0] on linux
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> from cryptography.hazmat.backends import default_backend
>>> default_backend()
<OpenSSLBackend(version: OpenSSL 3.5.3 16 Sep 2025, FIPS: True, Legacy: True)>
```

Thanks in advance for any help!

# Steps to reproduce

## Jump into a container

```
docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD:/w" -w /w debian:trixie
```

## Start virtual environment, install prerequisites

```
apt update && apt install -y openssl python3 python3-venv vim wget build-essential
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install PyJWT cryptography
```

## Install FIPS module

As described [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/master/README-FIPS.md#download-and-build-a-validated-fips-provider).

```
wget https://www.openssl.org/source/openssl-3.1.2.tar.gz
tar -xf openssl-3.1.2.tar.gz
cd openssl-3.1.2
./Configure enable-fips
make
make install_fips
```

## Control test

```
python test.py  # expect success
```

Expected output:
```
(.venv) root@4ea79d5dcc51:/w# python test.py
FIPS: False
success
```

## Test with FIPS enabled

```
OPENSSL_CONF=fips.cnf python test.py  # expect ES256 success, but RS256 failure
```

Expected output:
```
(.venv) root@4ea79d5dcc51:/w# OPENSSL_CONF=fips.cnf python test.py
FIPS: True
RS256 failed:
Unknown OpenSSL error. This error is commonly encountered
                    when another library is not cleaning up the OpenSSL error
                    stack. If you are using cryptography with another library
                    that uses OpenSSL try disabling it before reporting a bug.
                    Otherwise please file an issue at
                    https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues with
                    information on how to reproduce this. (error:0308010C:digital envelope routines:inner_evp_generic_fetch:unsupported:crypto/evp/evp_fetch.c:375:Global default library context, Algorithm (SHA256 : 102), Properties (), error:03000086:digital envelope routines:evp_md_init_internal:initialization error:crypto/evp/digest.c:271:)
```

## test.py

```python
from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidSignature, InternalError
from cryptography.hazmat.backends.openssl.backend import backend
from jwt.algorithms import get_default_algorithms

print('FIPS:', backend._fips_enabled)

failures = 0

verifier = get_default_algorithms()["ES256"]
pk = verifier.from_jwk({
    "kty":"EC",
    "crv":"P-256",
    "x":"MKBCTNIcKUSDii11ySs3526iDZ8AiTo7Tu6KPAqv7D4",
    "y":"4Etl6SRW2YiLUrN5vfvVHuhp7x8PxltmWWlbbM4IFyM",
    "use":"sig",
    "kid":"1",
})
try:
    verifier.verify(b"some message", pk, b"invalid signature")
except InvalidSignature:
    pass  # We don't have a valid signature, so expect this to fail.
except InternalError as e:
    print('ES256 failed:')
    print(e)
    failures += 1

verifier = get_default_algorithms()["RS256"]
```

title: New cffi>=2.0 pin makes cryptography incompatible with other libraries
need_summary: The developer asked if newer cryptography versions (which include security fixes) could be used alongside the existing cffi<2.0 pin, and the answer confirmed that version 46.0.0 works as a workaround.
security_topic: dependency version compatibility affecting security updates
question_text: Is there a world in which both versions are allowed?
answer_text: 46.0.0 does work, yes - for now there are workarounds, the concern is around having to choose between using snowflake (and whatever other dependencies have strict pins on cffi) and having up to date cryptography fixes going forward.
thread_text:
ISSUE #13468: New cffi>=2.0 pin makes cryptography incompatible with other libraries
Author: gibsondan
Date: 2025-09-18T21:12:46Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
Just flagging that this change https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/pull/13448 makes new versions of cryptography incompatible with other packages that pin cffi<2.0 (the specific example that I'm aware of currently is snowflake-connector-python). 

Is there a world in which both versions are allowed?

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @reaperhulk 2025-09-18T21:38:07Z:
(Pasting this comment here as well since a separate issue is good for this discussion)

Does 46.0.0 work for you? The version bound was only py314 there.

More broadly, I’m not aware of a good answer to this situation, only tradeoffs to choose between. There is no way to express free threaded only dependencies and pip additionally has a constraint where it does not consider pre-release to match >=3.14. Once 3.14 is out we could consider shifting the pin back up to 3.14 but technically that’s still incorrect since we only need it on 3.14t.

Separately, cffi 2.0 is not a semantic versioned library though so compatibility should not be an issue and libraries bounding <2 are under a misapprehension. That said, I imagine you aren’t setting that bound, it’s some other dep.
---
[c2] @gibsondan 2025-09-18T21:40:10Z:
46.0.0 does work, yes - for now there are workarounds, the concern is around having to choose between using snowflake (and whatever other dependencies have strict pins on cffi) and having up to date cryptography fixes going forward. 

(I also filed an issue in the snowflake-connector-python repo, since i'm not sure if they have a good reason for their pin)
---
[c3] @alex 2025-09-18T21:40:13Z:
Has an issue/PR been send to snowflake?

As @reaperhulk said, we're kind of between a rock and a hard place here. Would like to find the best solution, but it's probably going to be a compromise either way. The more we can help other libraries raise their bounds, I think the more flexibility we'll have.

(Maybe another way to say this is: no matter what, other libraries that want to be 3.14t compatible will need to raise their bounds.)
---
[c4] @alex 2025-09-27T18:25:58Z:
Given that snowflake is the only project we've heard about haaving this issue, and this issue is _really_ on their end (they have a pin for no reason), I'm going to close this from our end.

If there are other projects with upper bounds where this is causing issues, please let us know and we can discuss if it warrants some other action.
---

title: Add binding for SSL_get0_group_name to support PQC key exchange group detection
need_summary: The developer needed to know if adding a binding for SSL_get0_group_name to expose negotiated TLS group names is acceptable, and the maintainers confirmed it by merging cryptography PR #13384 and pyOpenSSL PR #1442.
security_topic: retrieving negotiated TLS group name for PQC detection
question_text:
I would like to make contributions to both repositories:
1. **cryptography**: Add bindings for `SSL_get0_group_name`. I'm planning to add the binding following the patterns I see for similar functions. My understanding is that it may need appropriate version guards (OpenSSL 3.2+); and looking into how to implement it (looking at things like this which is not quite the same situation as mine): https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/5cf5edf1b36afc8400e5b6d3975d0b15380f3eff/src/cryptography/hazmat/backends/openssl/backend.py#L288.
2. **pyOpenSSL**: Expose this as a new method (e.g., `get_group_name()`) in the SSL module's Connection class, similar conceptually to `get_cipher_list()`.
answer_text:
`SSL_get0_group_name` returns a `char *` of the negotiated group name, but while it's not officially documented looking at the code it appears to be the group name as defined by the TLS specs. I would be okay with that being exposed here. Eventually this binding would also need to live in rust-openssl since we're migrating that direction over time as well, but we can land it here first.

Before we merge here we'd like to see the PR opened on the pyOpenSSL side though (knowing all tests will fail of course) so we can agree on the API and see how the binding will be consumed.
thread_text:
ISSUE #13349: Add binding for SSL_get0_group_name to support PQC key exchange group detection
Author: toddabrams
Date: 2025-08-24T18:23:45Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
# Background
I am a developer for a python tool which uses pyOpenSSL to initiate handshakes and probe servers to understand their level of TLS support. I am planning to extend this tool to capture post-quantum cryptography (PQC) readiness by detecting which key exchange groups are actually negotiated during connections.

Per [OpenSSL docs]( https://docs.openssl.org/3.5/man3/SSL_CTX_set1_curves/#history):

> Support for ML-KEM was added in OpenSSL 3.5.
> 
> OpenSSL 3.5 also introduces support for three hybrid ECDH PQ key exchange TLS groups: X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024.  

If the conditions are right, one of these hybrid key exchange groups may be used, and I'd like to be able to use pyOpenSSL to capture which group was actually negotiated.

From the [OpenSSL docs](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man3/SSL_CTX_set1_curves/#description), `SSL_get0_group_name` is preferred for this:

> See also [SSL_get0_group_name(3)](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man3/SSL_get0_group_name/) which returns the name of the negotiated group directly and is generally preferred over SSL_get_negotiated_group().

Here is a link to the openssl source for [SSL_get0_group_name](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/53eb2363a1e6336a40a64b3f7b9f09eca95fabef/ssl/s3_lib.c#L5244) and [PR where it was introduced](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/commit/68668243b176cd2bc53a83c6768d4f39930ba8ed) as of OpenSSL 3.2.

Note: While `SSL_get0_group_name` was introduced in OpenSSL 3.2, the hybrid PQC groups that motivate this request require OpenSSL 3.5.

# Request
I would like to make contributions to both repositories:
1. **cryptography**: Add bindings for `SSL_get0_group_name`. I'm planning to add the binding following the patterns I see for similar functions. My understanding is that it may need appropriate version guards (OpenSSL 3.2+); and looking into how to implement it (looking at things like this which is not quite the same situation as mine): https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/5cf5edf1b36afc8400e5b6d3975d0b15380f3eff/src/cryptography/hazmat/backends/openssl/backend.py#L288.

# Background
I am a developer for a python tool which uses pyOpenSSL to initiate handshakes and probe servers to understand their level of TLS support. I am planning to extend this tool to capture post-quantum cryptography (PQC) readiness by detecting which key exchange groups are actually negotiated during connections.

Per [OpenSSL docs]( https://docs.openssl.org/3.5/man3/SSL_CTX_set1_curves/#history):

> Support for ML-KEM was added in OpenSSL 3.5.
> 
> OpenSSL 3.5 also introduces support for three hybrid ECDH PQ key exchange TLS groups: X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024.  

If the conditions are right, one of these hybrid key exchange groups may be used, and I'd like to be able to use pyOpenSSL to capture which group was actually negotiated.

From the [OpenSSL docs](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man3/SSL_CTX_set1_curves/#description), `SSL_get0_group_name` is preferred for this:

> See also [SSL_get0_group_name(3)](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man3/SSL_get0_group_name/) which returns the name of the negotiated group directly and is generally preferred over SSL_get_negotiated_group().

Here is a link to the openssl source for [SSL_get0_group_name](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/53eb2363a1e6336a40a64b3f7b9f09eca95fabef/ssl/s3_lib.c#L5244) and [PR where it was introduced](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/commit/68668243b176cd2bc53a83c6768d4f39930ba8ed) as of OpenSSL 3.2.

Note: While `SSL_get0_group_name` was introduced in OpenSSL 3.2, the hybrid PQC groups that motivate this request require OpenSSL 3.5.

# Request
I would like to make contributions to both repositories:
1. **cryptography**: Add bindings for `SSL_get0_group_name`. I'm planning to add the binding following the patterns I see for similar functions. My understanding is that it may need appropriate version guards (OpenSSL 3.2+); and looking into how to implement it (looking at things like this which is not quite the same situation as mine): https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/5cf5edf1b36afc8400e5b6d3975d0b15380f3eff/src/cryptography/hazmat/backends/openssl/backend.py#L288. 
2. **pyOpenSSL**: Expose this as a new method (e.g., `get_group_name()`) in the SSL module's [Connection class](https://github.com/pyca/pyopenssl/blob/main/src/OpenSSL/SSL.py#L1948), similar conceptually to `get_cipher_list()`.

# Status

So far, I've:
- followed the [development docs](https://cryptography.io/en/latest/development/) and `nox -e local` succeeds in my local environment
- been reading through c-bindings.rst and ssl.py to understand how I would add a binding given that `SSL_get0_group_name` is only available 
- joined the `#pyca` IRC chat 

# Other discussions

I noticed there have been some similar-ish discussions, for example around setting curves: https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/10797. This was an approach I initially considered.

However, I noticed in the [release notes for OpenSSL 3.5.0](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/openssl-3.5/CHANGES.md#openssl-35) that it appears that at least one of the hybrid PQC groups, `X25519MLKEM768`, is now set by default:

> The default TLS group list setting is now set to: ?*X25519MLKEM768 / ?*X25519:?secp256r1 / ?X448:?secp384r1:?secp521r1 / ?ffdhe2048:?ffdhe3072
> 
> This means two key shares (X25519MLKEM768 and X25519) will be sent by default by the TLS client. GOST groups and FFDHE groups larger than 3072 bits are no longer enabled by default.

I'm a bit new to this area, but either:
a) This means that if a server is configured with `X25519MLKEM768` for the key change group, that my tool will initiate a handshake with it and the group would be negotiated preferentially.
b) Non-PQC groups would need to be excluded by using a setter such as `SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list`, in which case I'd need to make contributions for this method as well in both pyOpenSSL and cryptography.

title: CryptographyDeprecationWarning when parsing certifi bundle
need_summary: The deprecation warning for certificates with non‑positive serial numbers will stay until those CAs are removed from certifi, and you can suppress or filter it via Python’s warnings system (see https://docs.python.org/3/library/warnings.html#warnings.filterwarnings).
security_topic: deprecation timeline for certificate parsing warnings
question_text: It would just be appreciated if you could mention whether the depreciation period (i.e. before turning these warnings into errors) will last until the last “invalid” CAs from `certifi` will be rotated out.
answer_text: Yes, we will not end the deprecation period until these CAs are removed from certifi or other major trust stores.

comments.author: Rogdham
comments.body:
When running the following code:
```py
import certifi
from cryptography.x509 import load_pem_x509_certificates

load_pem_x509_certificates(certifi.contents().encode())
```

…the following warning is raised:
```
CryptographyDeprecationWarning: Parsed a serial number which wasn't positive (i.e., it was negative or zero), which is disallowed by RFC 5280. Loading this certificate will cause an exception in a future release of cryptography.
```

I believe this was introduced in #12853.

I'm opening this issue because I think you would like to get the feedback, because parsing CAs included in `certifi` seems like a reasonable use case. But I understand that this may not be an issue in `cryptography` per se, so feel free to redirect me elsewhere.

---

Versions used:
```
$ uv pip freeze
certifi==2025.8.3
cffi==1.17.1
cryptography==45.0.6
idna==3.10
pycparser==2.22
```

comments.author: nbastin
comments.body:
Unrelated to the web PKI trust store, but related to cryptography parsing of these bundles - AMD VCEK certs are _required_ to have a serial number of zero.  Even if they change this in a future revision users will be dealing with those certs for SEV-SNP attestation for existing processors for their lifetime.

We also have plenty of certs on industrial devices that have negative serial numbers (valid under X.509).  Perhaps SN validation should be deferred to the point of verification?  Or maybe a separate hook for parse validation policy?

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
Someone tell AMD that that's categorically not compatible with RFC 5280, which is fairly unambiguous:

> The serial number MUST be a positive integer assigned by the CA to each certificate.

Negative serial numbers are not valid.

comments.author: nbastin
comments.body: RFC 5280 is for internet PKI, none of these uses are internet PKI.  X.509 (ISO/IEC 9594-8) unambiguously sets SN ranges as ```INTEGER (0..MAX)``` and previous revisions just had it as an integer, where negative was clearly valid.
