title: Since 45.0, `load_pem_private_key` allows arbitrary garbage after `-----END PRIVATE KEY-----`
need_summary: The developer asked whether accepting arbitrary data after the PEM END line is a security issue, and the maintainer answered that RFC 7468 permits such data (see RFC 7468 §2).
security_topic: PEM parsing permissiveness for trailing data
question_text: Maybe it's intentional, but it feels like something that might not have been intentional so I'm reporting it (can't hurt).
answer_text: The current behaviour is (arguably) correct. RFC 7468 makes clear that any data before encapsulation boundaries is permitted (and states parsers MUST NOT malfunction when processing such data - see section 2).
thread_text:
ISSUE #13125: Since 45.0, `load_pem_private_key` allows arbitrary garbage after `-----END PRIVATE KEY-----`
Author: bluetech
Date: 2025-07-01T12:17:40Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
Since version 45.0, `load_pem_private_key` accepts arbitrary "garbage" after the `-----END PRIVATE KEY-----` line. Previous versions would fail with the error below. Maybe it's intentional, but it feels like something that *might* not have been intentional so I'm reporting it (can't hurt). It doesn't affect me personally, I only noticed it because I have a test case which tries to make a PEM private key input invalid by appending `b"xxx"` to it which no longer fails (though I should note that it seems adding `b"\nxxx"` doesn't fail in previous versions either).

Example code:

```py
import os

from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import serialization


PRIVATE_KEY = b"""-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----
MIGHAgEAMBMGByqGSM49AgEGCCqGSM49AwEHBG0wawIBAQQglcJB9Do845/R18ef
ButMVXFbRqmo/F9kdsIbgTSbDUWhRANCAAR+OeTq+FCd8eRNt9IU16kP3SZ5W8Pj
dS0YwItKLwTyDA4zTupEPWWqAikmw7Xv9DAgiDVFLbzP3C+3mjYmvUkL
-----END PRIVATE KEY-----"""

# OK
serialization.load_pem_private_key(PRIVATE_KEY, password=None)

# Previously would fail, now passes
serialization.load_pem_private_key(PRIVATE_KEY + os.urandom(1000), password=None)
```

Error in 44:

```
ValueError: ('Could not deserialize key data. The data may be in an incorrect format, the provided password may be incorrect, it may be encrypted with an unsupported algorithm, or it may be an unsupported key type (e.g. EC curves with explicit parameters).', [<OpenSSLError(code=503841036, lib=60, reason=524556, reason_text=unsupported)>])
```

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @alex 2025-07-01T12:27:49Z:
Hmm, interesting -- I'm surprised that garbage was previously rejected. Historically most of the bugs we've gotten are that we've been _too strict_, and we specifically loosened PEM parsing as a result of that.
---
[c2] @bluetech 2025-07-01T13:00:33Z:
Yes I thought it might be intentional.

I was thinking about suggesting a "strict" mode but it isn't worth it IMO.

Either way, it's a bad idea to store or forward user PEM inputs directly, instead should load+serialize and store that instead (preferably in DER format).
---
[c3] @nbastin 2025-07-10T00:32:14Z:
As a person who every once in a while pops up to be one of the squeaky wheels here, the current behaviour is (arguably) correct.  RFC 7468 (which is more of a reflection of reality at the time than an actual spec, which never existed during the time when many of these systems were built) makes clear that _any_ data before encapsulation boundaries is permitted (and states parsers MUST NOT malfunction when processing such data - [section 2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7468#section-2)).  It is ambiguous as to whether data is "before" an encapsulation boundary if you never find another `BEGIN`, but plenty of systems generate such files and thus failing to parse them puts a burden on users.
---

ButMVXFbRqmo/F9kdsIbgTSbDUWhRANCAAR+OeTq+FCd8eRNt9IU16kP3SZ5W8Pj
dS0YwItKLwTyDA4zTupEPWWqAikmw7Xv9DAgiDVFLbzP3C+3mjYmvUkL
-----END PRIVATE KEY-----"""

# OK
serialization.load_pem_private_key(PRIVATE_KEY, password=None)

# Previously would fail, now passes
serialization.load_pem_private_key(PRIVATE_KEY + os.urandom(1000), password=None)
```

Error in 44:

```
ValueError: ('Could not deserialize key data. The data may be in an incorrect format, the provided password may be incorrect, it may be encrypted with an unsupported algorithm, or it may be an unsupported key type (e.g. EC curves with explicit parameters).', [<OpenSSLError(code=503841036, lib=60, reason=524556, reason_text=unsupported)>])
```

comments.author: alex
comments.body: Hmm, interesting -- I'm surprised that garbage was previously rejected. Historically most of the bugs we've gotten are that we've been _too strict_, and we specifically loosened PEM parsing as a result of that.

comments.author: bluetech
comments.body:
Yes I thought it might be intentional.

I was thinking about suggesting a "strict" mode but it isn't worth it IMO.

Either way, it's a bad idea to store or forward user PEM inputs directly, instead should load+serialize and store that instead (preferably in DER format).

comments.author: nbastin
comments.body: As a person who every once in a while pops up to be one of the squeaky wheels here, the current behaviour is (arguably) correct.  RFC 7468 (which is more of a reflection of reality at the time than an actual spec, which never existed during the time when many of these systems were built) makes clear that _any_ data before encapsulation boundaries is permitted (and states parsers MUST NOT malfunction when processing such data - [section 2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7468#section-2)).  It is ambiguous as to whether data is "before" an encapsulation boundary if you never find another `BEGIN`, but plenty of systems generate such files and thus failing to parse them puts a burden on users.

title: Massive request slowdown in django webserver when cryptography is installed (running in docker)
need_summary: The developer needed to know which dependency caused the request slowdown when cryptography is installed, and the answer points to the google-auth-library-python package (see its google/auth/crypt/_cryptography_rsa.py file) as the source of the issue.
security_topic: request slowdown due to cryptography dependency in Django
question_text:
Hello,

I have been trying to troubleshoot an issue with my web application running with django where most requests are taking seconds and sometimes minutes instead of milliseconds to run. It also gets worse the longer the server is running.

In the end I boiled it down to the cryptography module. The issue arises when only installing cryptography onto the sane version, and I emphasize on that fact that it only takes a `pip install`, nothing else. Not even an import in the application is needed.

It had initially been added to the server as a requirement for allowing SSO logins in a recent update.

I am running:
python3.11 from python:3.11-slim-bookworm
Django==5.1.9
cryptography==45.0.4

The issue also occurred when trying other images such as:
- python:3.11-slim-bullseye
- python:3.11-bookworm
- python:3.11-bullseye

I also tried both with the pip binary and with --no-binary enabled and an up to date rust toolchain installed.
I tried running an older version of cryptography (41.0.7).
The slowdown is always happening when cryptography is installed no matter what I tried.

Thank you
answer_text:
Hello, 

Thanks for your suggestion @alex, I looked into packages using cryptography optionally, and after doing some tracing I found the package indirectly responsible.
It is the google-auth-library-python, and the slowdown is caused when loading the credential json used for instantiating a bucket client connection, from the trace most time was spent in this file.

However, the real problem is coming from the fact that my code is re-instantiating a bucket client connection on most requests. 
I suspect that this problem was previously hidden either:
1. because the cryptography fallback methods used without cryptography were faster (it takes 0.3 seconds on average with cryptography)
2. because of some caching capabilities of credentials or clients by the google auth library only available when not using cryptography

In any case my issue is resolved by simply avoiding to recreate bucket clients unnecessarily so I will close the issue.
Thank you for your time.

title: Cryptography parsed the CRL file with an empty Key Identifier.
need_summary: Developer asked whether an empty AuthorityKeyIdentifier extension in a CRL violates RFC 5280 and poses a security issue; the maintainer answered that RFC 5280 does not explicitly forbid an empty AKI and cited the relevant RFC section as the basis.
security_topic: whether empty AuthorityKeyIdentifier extension violates RFC 5280
question_text: Is there some place that says this violates an RFC?
answer_text: I'm not sure that it does. RFC 5280 does not explicitly state that the AKI extension sequence must not be empty—it only specifies that the IDP extension must not be an empty sequence. According to RFC 5280, the AKI extension may be based on the key identifier (the subject key identifier in the issuer's certificate) or the issuer name and serial number.
thread_text:
ISSUE #13051: Cryptography parsed the CRL file with an empty Key Identifier.
Author: onepeople158
Date: 2025-06-07T14:47:11Z
Labels: waiting-on-reporter, Stale
State: closed

[c0]
Version: 45.0.3

Hello Developer, I successfully parsed a CRL file with an empty Key Identifier using Cryptography.When I used GnuTLS to parse this CRL file, it returned an error: error: gnutls_x509_ext_import_authority_key_id: ASN1 parser: Error in DER parsing. Is this considered an error?

Test Case:

[crl_empty_key.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/20639268/crl_empty_key.zip)

Code:
```
from cryptography.x509 import load_pem_x509_crl, load_der_x509_crl
from cryptography.x509 import ExtensionNotFound
import sys

def load_crl(file_path):
    with open(file_path, "rb") as f:
        crl_data = f.read()
    try:
        crl = load_pem_x509_crl(crl_data)
    except ValueError:
        crl = load_der_x509_crl(crl_data)
    return crl

def print_crl_issuer(file_path):
    crl=load_crl(file_path)
    aki_extension = None
    try:
        for ext in crl.extensions:
             if ext.oid == x509.oid.ExtensionOID.AUTHORITY_KEY_IDENTIFIER:
                    aki=ext.value
                    print(aki)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error parsing CRL: {e}")

file_path = 'filename'
print_crl_issuer(file_path)
```

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @alex 2025-06-07T16:38:01Z:
Hmm, so an empty AKI is stupid, but it's not clear it violates the RFC?

```
   AuthorityKeyIdentifier ::= SEQUENCE {
      keyIdentifier             [0] KeyIdentifier           OPTIONAL,
      authorityCertIssuer       [1] GeneralNames            OPTIONAL,
      authorityCertSerialNumber [2] CertificateSerialNumber OPTIONAL  }
```

(https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5280#section-4.2.1.1)

Is there some place that says this violates an RFC?
---
[c2] @onepeople158 2025-06-08T08:32:23Z:
> Hmm, so an empty AKI is stupid, but it's not clear it violates the RFC?
> 
> ```
>    AuthorityKeyIdentifier ::= SEQUENCE {
>       keyIdentifier             [0] KeyIdentifier           OPTIONAL,
>       authorityCertIssuer       [1] GeneralNames            OPTIONAL,
>       authorityCertSerialNumber [2] CertificateSerialNumber OPTIONAL  }
> ```
> 
> (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5280#section-4.2.1.1)
> 
> Is there some place that says this violates an RFC?

Hello, I created an empty AuthorityKeyIdentifier (AKI) extension where all three subfields are Null. Cryptography accepted this CRL file. Does this violate the following statement in RFC 5280:

> [The identification can be based on either the key identifier (the subject key identifier in the CRL signer's certificate) or the issuer name and serial number.](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5280#section-4.2.1.1:~:text=The%20identification%20MAY%20be%20based%20on%20either%20the%0A%20%20%20key%20identifier%20(the%20subject%20key%20identifier%20in%20the%20issuer%27s%0A%20%20%20certificate)%20or%20the%20issuer%20name%20and%20serial%20number.)

[empty_aki.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/20643477/empty_aki.zip)
---
[c3] @onepeople158 2025-06-09T02:27:57Z:
> I'm not sure that it does.

Hello, the use of an empty sequence for the AKI extension is unreasonable. However, RFC 5280 does not explicitly state that the AKI extension sequence must not be empty—it only specifies that the IDP extension must not be an empty sequence. According to RFC 5280, the AKI extension [may be based on the key identifier (the subject key identifier in the issuer certificate) or the issuer name and serial number](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5280#section-4.2.1.1:~:text=The%20identification%20MAY%20be%20based%20on%20either%20the%0A%20%20%20key%20identifier%20(the%20subject%20key%20identifier%20in%20the%20issuer%27s%0A%20%20%20certificate)%20or%20the%20issuer%20name%20and%20serial%20number.).
---
[c4] @alex 2025-06-09T02:31:55Z:
I think that's a good summary, the fact that they use the ALL CAPS MAY means that MAY carries this definition:

```
MAY   This word, or the adjective "OPTIONAL", mean that an item is
   truly optional.  One vendor may choose to include the item because a
   particular marketplace requires it or because the vendor feels that
   it enhances the product while another vendor may omit the same item.
   An implementation which does not include a particular option MUST be
   prepared to interoperate with another implementation which does
   include the option, though perhaps with reduced functionality. In the
   same vein an implementation which does include a particular option
   MUST be prepared to interoperate with another implementation which
   does not include the option (except, of course, for the feature the
   option provides.)
```

Which seems to indicate it's not required to be?

The whole RFC is written in a confusing way. Unless there's a clear reason our behavior either a) violates the spec, b) harms interoperability, c) is a security issue, I'd be inclined to leave it as is.

title: Can't parse PKCS#12 as DER
need_summary: The PKCS#12 DER parsing warning is a deprecation concern, and the maintainers will address it under issue #12936 (https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/12936).
security_topic: PKCS#12 DER parsing warning
question_text: Am I the only one getting this notice?
answer_text: (I'm going to close this and track it as part of https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/12936. Thank you for reporting this)

comments.author: nsymms
comments.body:
cryptography v45.0.3.

> /home/vscode/.local/lib/python3.12/site-packages/requests_pkcs12.py:42: UserWarning: PKCS#12 bundle could not be parsed as DER, falling back to parsing as BER. Please file an issue at https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues explaining how your PKCS#12 bundle was created. In the future, this may become an exception.
>   private_key, cert, ca_certs = cryptography.hazmat.primitives.serialization.pkcs12.load_key_and_certificates(..)

I'm using the requests_pkcs12 module, but I also tried pkcs12.load_key_and_certificates() directly, both give the message.

My PKCS12 certificate (a PFX file) was created directly by the certificate vendor, OATI (www.oati.com / www.oaticerts.com).  So I'm not sure how the bundle was created.  OATI is a major certificate vendor for the wholesale electricity industry.  Most every electric grid operator (ISO / RTO) in the US requires an OATI certificate to access their systems.

I didn't see any other issues on this besides the placeholder waiting for related issues.  Am I the only one getting this notice?

Thanks

comments.author: reaperhulk
comments.body: So far you're the first reporter, yes. Thanks for the information about the source. I don't suppose your org has a relationship with OATI such that you can file an issue with them asking them to encode their PKCS12 as DER rather than BER?

comments.author: nsymms
comments.body:
I'll certainly ask about it, but we really don't have much influence.  I'm pretty sure OATI would be concerned with causing issues to their existing userbase and those systems not being able to work with changes to the certificate format.  Most people in the industry use java and I have no idea how the popular java libraries treat the PKCS12 standards.

For my use case, I guess I'll be using openssl to convert the OATI certs to DER encoding in the future.

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
Fortunately there should be no compatibility risk: DER is a subset of BER, so people's existing BER parsers will work fine with DER.

One of our big questions is whether they're using some popular open source (or commercial) library for generating the PKCS#12 bundles, in which case we'd really want to get it fixed upstream.

comments.author: alex
comments.body: Ok, that uses indefinite length encoding, so very clearly BER. If you're able to get a more recent one, that'd be great -- concurrently I'll ask around.

comments.author: alex
comments.body: Thanks for digging this up. We expect this to be a long deprecation, so we're going to see what we can do here.

comments.author: alex
comments.body: (I'm going to close this and track it as part of https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/12936. Thank you for reporting this)

title: [Feature request] Allow to define tag length for object AESGCM
need_summary: The developer needed to know how to configure a 12-byte GCM authentication tag in the cryptography library, and the answer referenced the cryptography.io GCM mode documentation as the concrete source.
security_topic: setting custom AES-GCM tag length in cryptography library
question_text: I'm working with DLMS protocol ... It uses AES GCM 128 encryption for secure communication. I would like to use cryptography lib to decrypt those DLMS payloads, but it's not possible, because when I create a cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead.AESGCM object, I'm not allowed to set the tag length to 12 bytes, it uses hard coded 16 bytes. (12 bytes is defined on DLMS standard) ... But would be nice not having to manage two cryptography libs.
answer_text: Tag lengths can be set using the more flexible https://cryptography.io/en/latest/hazmat/primitives/symmetric-encryption/#cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.modes.GCM API. While the one-shot AEAD is preferrable where possible, this API is more general.
thread_text:
ISSUE #13030: [Feature request] Allow to define tag length for object AESGCM
Author: braquino
Date: 2025-06-03T10:15:35Z
Labels: waiting-on-reporter
State: closed

[c0]
Hello,

I'm working with DLMS protocol: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEC_62056

It uses AES GCM 128 encryption for secure comunication.
I would like to use cryptography lib to decrypt those DLMS payloads, but it's not possible, because when I create a `cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead.AESGCM` object, I'm not allowed to set the tag length to 12 bytes, it uses hard coded 16 bytes.
(12 bytes is defined on DLMS standard)

Looking at the Rust code, seems that the Rust struct allows the length setting, but the python wrapper doesn't.

As a workaround I'm using pycryptodome:

``` python
from Crypto.Cipher import AES
cipher = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_GCM, nonce=nonce, mac_len=12)
```

But would be nice not having to manage two cryptography libs.

Thank you in advance.

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @alex 2025-06-03T10:19:53Z:
Tag lengths can be set using the more flexible https://cryptography.io/en/latest/hazmat/primitives/symmetric-encryption/#cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.modes.GCM API. While the one-shot AEAD is preferrable where possible, this API si more general.
---
[c2] @braquino 2025-06-03T10:30:24Z:
Ok, thank you, it works
```python
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers import (
  Cipher, algorithms, modes
)
decryptor = Cipher(
    algorithms.AES(key),
    modes.GCM(nonce, gcm_tag, min_tag_length=12),
).decryptor()

decryptor.authenticate_additional_data(aad)
plain = decryptor.update(ciphertext) + decryptor.finalize()
```
---

title: Unable to load private unencrypted key in `45.0.3` which worked in `44.0.3`
need_summary: The developer needed to know why loading an unencrypted RSA private key fails in version 45.x and whether it’s a security regression; the maintainer explained it’s due to using PKCS#8 keys with incorrect PEM headers per the PKCS#8 RFC (see the RFC and related issue #12993).
security_topic: key format compliance and regression policy
question_text: No problem! @alex, would this be considered a regression that will be fixed in an upcoming release or are users expected to modify their private keys so that the headers match what is expected by PKCS#8?
answer_text: Strictly speaking this is part of the PKCS#8 RFC, so we don't really consider it a bug -- if this was _super_ widespread we might add a temporary workaround. We're thinking about if there's a docs/error message improvement we could make here.

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
The issue here is that you have a PKCS#8 key and the PEM headers are `BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY`, however PKCS#8 keys are supposed to have a `BEGIN PRIVATE KEY` header. https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/12993 is a similar issue.

How was this PEM generated? Is there some library you used, or was it constructed "manually"

comments.author: joshdcu
comments.body:
Yes, you're exactly right, thank you! The key is generated by the `crypto/rsa` Go library but I add the headers "manually" so it's the same issue you linked to. Switching to `BEGIN PRIVATE KEY` solves the issue:

title: Can adding some bindings (for OpenSSL-3.x) enable support for SM2?
need_summary: The developer asked if adding OpenSSL‑3.x bindings could enable SM2 support, and the maintainer replied that it requires explicit implementation, pointing to the proposed API in PR #5894 as the concrete reference.
security_topic: SM2 algorithm support in cryptography library
question_text: At https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/commit/c28bfb352ab1f390900ef92856a9570aadd5fe2c, we can use EVP_PKEY_set_alias_type  API to using SM2 algorithms. However, the latest version has removed these APIs. Is there any other way to make cryptography support the SM2 algorithm?
answer_text:
We no longer have workarounds for using unsupported features like this. To use SM2 in cryptography we'd need to implement support explicitly. It would likely look like the API proposed in https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/pull/5894 but using the rust-openssl bindings like we do in our current codebase. If you want to contribute a PR I'd be willing to review, but there are a few things we'll require:
* SM2 keys should **not** be allowed to be used with ECDSA and should instead only use a `sign` method on their objects that supports `SM2Sign`. I want to see a concrete use case before allowing ECDSA signing. These keys should not be registered against the EC key types.
* SM2 signing should only work with SM3 hashing per spec.

question_text: So I'd suggest to revisit that deprecation.

import certifi

title: Remove BER in PKCS#7 and PKCS#12
need_summary: The developer asked if retaining BER parsing in PKCS#7/PKCS#12 poses a security risk and when it will be removed; the maintainers answered that the warning is now more detailed (see commit f5802fe7e08774cb8f8d80ede396de91efb1afca) and that OpenSSL BER codepaths will be dropped after version 45.0.0, providing a concrete mitigation timeline.
security_topic: risk assessment of BER parsing in PKCS#7/PKCS#12 handling
question_text: I don't fully understand the issue to be reported -- can you explain or point to a doc explaining the issue? Is it an issue only for users of the cryptography library going forward, or does it pose a risk to the issuing CA? Are we talking about a MITM exploiting BER to execute arbitrary code during parsing?
answer_text: The concern here is that it requires us to retain a BER parser. Basically every modern cryptographic protocol uses DER (which is a subset of BER and is more rigid). In our case, we have a Rust (memory safe) DER parser, and rely on OpenSSL (memory unsafe) for BER parsing. We'd like to migrate PKCS#7 to our Rust DER parser, but can't do that as long as we need to support BER. There's no particular risk to the issuer here, but we think most folks will want to do the right thing and just use DER -- there's no real reason not to.
thread_text:
ISSUE #12936: Remove BER in PKCS#7 and PKCS#12
Author: alex
Date: 2025-05-18T15:26:55Z
Labels: 
State: open

[c0]
Starting in 45.0.0, we emit warnings on PKCS#7/PKCS#12 that are parsed by OpenSSL but not by our own DER parser. We are now in the "waiting to see how many people file issues" phase.

Once a sufficient period of time/low issue volume has been established, we will remove the OpenSSL codepaths entirely.

## Trackers for filed issues

### PKCS#7

- [ ] Australian Taxation Office
- [ ] Sectigo (Invalid SET ordering)
- [ ] Microsoft ActiveDirectory Certificate Services CA (Invalid SET ordering)
- [ ] Italian Identity Card
- [ ] ...

### PKCS#12

- [ ] Apple Pay Payment Token (https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/13034)
- [ ] Spanish Government (https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/12936#issuecomment-3693356008)
- [ ] Bypass (https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/14386)
- [ ] ...

--- COMMENTS ---

[c4] @alex 2025-08-29T21:43:47Z:
The concern here is that it requires us to retain a BER parser. Basically every modern cryptographic protocol uses DER (which is a subset of BER and is more rigid).

In our case, we have a Rust (memory safe) DER parser, and rely on OpenSSL (memory unsafe) for BER parsing. We'd like to migrate PKCS#7 to our Rust DER parser, but can't do that as long as we need to support BER. There's no particular risk to the issuer here, but we think most folks will want to do the right thing and just use DER -- there's no real reason not to.

[c22] @TaaviE 2025-12-12T14:50:41Z:
Looking into this more it seems like Outlook S/MIME signing outputs a PKCS#7 structure with indefinite length `EncapsulatedContentInfo` even if no `eContent` is used in the `SEQUENCE`.

The [CMS RFC](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5652) says the following:

> Signed attributes and authenticated attributes are the only data types used in the CMS that require DER encoding.

The section about `EncapsulatedContentInfo` says:

>   The content is represented in the type EncapsulatedContentInfo
>      eContentType is an object identifier.  The object identifier uniquely specifies the content type.
>      eContent is the content itself, carried as an octet string.  The eContent need not be DER encoded.

While it is somewhat lazy that Outlook doesn't use definite lengths on `.p7s` S/MIME signatures (with no `eContent`), it seems to be correct based on the CMS RFC. Which means that if `cryptography` removes BER fallback it will likely make S/MIME PKCS#7 very annoying to handle. Even if it's for example just to read the certificates within.

Having a memory-safe fallback BER parser would keep this use-case functional.

Honestly, I think expecting PKCS#7 and PKCS#12 to only use DER is unrealistic.  At least in the case of CMS (PKCS#7’s successor), using DER is explicitly not required by the standard.

It might be okay to expect DER when one knows how the message is created, or when one is creating a new application and does not need to work with existing messages.  However, a general-purpose library needs to support full BER.  It’s definitely possible for a Rust parser to support arbitrary BER, though.

[c28] @DemiMarie 2026-01-21T19:59:46Z:
> There's no particular risk to the issuer here, but we think most folks will want to do the right thing and just use DER -- there's no real reason not to.

There actually is.  BER can be generated in one pass without having to buffer the entire message in memory, whereas DER does not support this.  This also makes serializing BER significantly simpler than serializing DER.

BER parsing is definitely more complex than DER parsing, but if one maintains a stack of unclosed tags I suspect it is not too difficult.  I prototyped an (untested, never run) C implementation and might be willing to contribute a Rust implementation.

Some countersignatures in CAdES (which is very widely used in Europe) are taken over the original signature, however it happened to be encoded.  Going from BER to DER would corrupt it.  The standard mentions that DER _should_ be used, but that is not a requirement.  One of the goals of CAdES is long-term storage, so I expect that implementations will be expected to support signatures that did not use DER.

> So in general, applications that need to tolerate BER should handle that complexity themselves. Maybe share a common shim for a format. But this complexity should remain in those applications instead of being brought into pyca
> 
> Dropping checks sounds like the most harmful way of providing compatibility.

I think the vast majority of use-cases need to handle full BER.  An implementation that only supports DER is not an implementation of PKCS\#7/CMS or of PKCS\#12, but rather only of a subset of those standards that does not include many uses people have no choice but to use.

Apple code signatures don’t use DER.  Neither do EJBCA or ADCS exports, nor do various other things that people don’t have any chance of changing.  In particular, anything based on BouncyCastle does not use DER.  Unless an application _knows_ that it only needs DER support, then it will need to pull in that shim.

Arguably, RSA Security and the IETF made a mistake when they defined PKCS\#7/CMS and PKCS\#12, but it’s too late to change that.  There’s simply too much data already in the wild that needs to be handled, and the users of pyca/cryptography simply don’t have the ability to change those who produce non-DER data.

Which is totally fair and very likely much more suitable for each use-case than trying to provide a generic "kitchen sink". In general not knowing what you need and cryptography aren't a good mix in the first place. In that sense a manual toggle "I want (legacy) BER" would be fair while OSSL fallbacks exist. But again, shouldn't be the default.
---

```python
import base64

from cryptography import x509
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.serialization import pkcs7
from pydantic import BaseModel


class CertificateResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    p7: str
    p10: str
    credentialToken: str
    links: list[dict[str, str]]

    def decode_certificate_chain(self) -> list[x509.Certificate]:
        """Returns certificate chain contained in `p7` field.

        >>> certificate = CertificateResponse(id=0, p7="", p10="...", credentialToken="...", links=[{"...": "..."}])
        >>> certificates = certificate.decode_certificate_chain()
        >>> certificates
        [<Certificate(subject=<Name(C=AU,O=mygovid.gov.au,CN=poi id,2.5.4.46=6a4aba42-b897-4478-b983-678f2bad1821)>, ...)>, <Certificate(subject=<Name(C=AU,O=Australian Taxation Office,OU=Certification Authority,CN=ATO Sub Certification Authority)>, ...)>, <Certificate(subject=<Name(C=AU,O=Australian Taxation Office,OU=Certification Authority,CN=ATO Root Certification Authority)>, ...)>]
        """
        return pkcs7.load_der_pkcs7_certificates(base64.standard_b64decode(self.p7))
```

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
The concern here is that it requires us to retain a BER parser. Basically every modern cryptographic protocol uses DER (which is a subset of BER and is more rigid).

In our case, we have a Rust (memory safe) DER parser, and rely on OpenSSL (memory unsafe) for BER parsing. We'd like to migrate PKCS#7 to our Rust DER parser, but can't do that as long as we need to support BER. There's no particular risk to the issuer here, but we think most folks will want to do the right thing and just use DER -- there's no real reason not to.

I've encountered this with S/MIME (`smime.p7s`) generated by Outlook (Classic). The .p7s contains "DigiCert Assured ID Root G2", "DigiCert Assured G2 SMIME RSA4096 SHA384 2024 CA1" and one personal certificate under that CA.

Using latest `master` (https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/commit/50c9a7c2428c8b2f63b027616790895fbb673c39) it gives the following error:

```
 ValueError: error parsing asn1 value: ParseError { kind: InvalidLength }
```

comments.author: TaaviE
comments.body:
Looking into this more it seems like Outlook S/MIME signing outputs a PKCS#7 structure with indefinite length `EncapsulatedContentInfo` even if no `eContent` is used in the `SEQUENCE`.

The [CMS RFC](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5652) says the following:

> Signed attributes and authenticated attributes are the only data types used in the CMS that require DER encoding.

The section about `EncapsulatedContentInfo` says:

>   The content is represented in the type EncapsulatedContentInfo
>      eContentType is an object identifier.  The object identifier uniquely specifies the content type.
>      eContent is the content itself, carried as an octet string.  The eContent need not be DER encoded.

While it is somewhat lazy that Outlook doesn't use definite lengths on `.p7s` S/MIME signatures (with no `eContent`), it seems to be correct based on the CMS RFC. Which means that if `cryptography` removes BER fallback it will likely make S/MIME PKCS#7 very annoying to handle. Even if it's for example just to read the certificates within.

Having a memory-safe fallback BER parser would keep this use-case functional.

comments.author: DemiMarie
comments.body:
Honestly, I think expecting PKCS#7 and PKCS#12 to only use DER is unrealistic.  At least in the case of CMS (PKCS#7’s successor), using DER is explicitly not required by the standard.

It might be okay to expect DER when one knows how the message is created, or when one is creating a new application and does not need to work with existing messages.  However, a general-purpose library needs to support full BER.  It’s definitely possible for a Rust parser to support arbitrary BER, though.

comments.author: DemiMarie
comments.body:
> There's no particular risk to the issuer here, but we think most folks will want to do the right thing and just use DER -- there's no real reason not to.

There actually is.  BER can be generated in one pass without having to buffer the entire message in memory, whereas DER does not support this.  This also makes serializing BER significantly simpler than serializing DER.

BER parsing is definitely more complex than DER parsing, but if one maintains a stack of unclosed tags I suspect it is not too difficult.  I prototyped an (untested, never run) C implementation and might be willing to contribute a Rust implementation.

comments.author: TaaviE
comments.body:
> At least in the case of CMS (PKCS#7’s successor), using DER is explicitly not required by the standard.

While CMS indeed explicitly allows the use of BER, using it is technically really not necessary. Anyone reasonable would remove it with the next iteration of the standard. 

> There actually is. BER can be generated in one pass without having to buffer the entire message in memory, whereas DER does not support this. This also makes serializing BER significantly simpler than serializing DER.

Not only is it unnecessary, the reason for allowing it is a "sacrifice" for some hypothetical. Single-pass generation is both limiting and very niche. I heavily doubt something like that even exists in reality, even if it does, it should not dictate the entire ecosystem.

DER support for CMS is necessary for compatibility with existing legacy systems, that's it. Nor should that support be enabled by default or written in an memory-unsafe language.

comments.author: DemiMarie
comments.body: It’s definitely possible to parse BER in a memory-safe language.  I think it would be easier to parse BER in Rust than to convince the existing institutions generating non-DER BER to switch to generating DER, not to mention the existing data already in the wild.

comments.author: TaaviE
comments.body: Certainly, it's not in the scope of pyca/cryptography to go and change standards or convince any relevant parties. Just the defaults should be good, memory-safe and encourage better designs.

comments.author: DemiMarie
comments.body:
@TaaviE CMS Advanced Electronic Signatures has signatures over BER-encoded data.

I totally agree that any new users of CMS should use DER, and it makes sense to only support _creating_ DER-encoded signatures.  I also believe that issues should be filed with anything that does not produce DER.  But there are a lot of existing BER-encoded signatures in the wild.

comments.author: DemiMarie
comments.body:
I think a good first step would be to drop the checks for invalid SET ordering and minimal-length encodings when parsing PKCS7, except for signed and authenticated attributes, CRLs, and certificates (which must be DER) or if the user explicitly requests DER (required for RPKI).  That adds minimal implmentation complexity.

Supporting indefinite length encodings requires maintaining a stack, but otherwise it should be possible to have an API quite close to what a DER decoder provides.

comments.author: DemiMarie
comments.body: It appears that some BSI standards actually _require_ not being complient with DER.  See <https://github.com/Keyfactor/ejbca-ce/issues/1028#issuecomment-4010896604>.

comments.author: TaaviE
comments.body:
> CMS Advanced Electronic Signatures has signatures over BER-encoded data.
> It appears that some BSI standards actually require not being complient with DER.

Not every use-case needs to be supported considering the maintenance burden. I'm sure there are even more bespoke complex use-cases out there that could be found. Looking at CAdES, it also seems like the signature is (very reasonably) over DER not BER, to be deterministic. The outer structure can be BER, thus it can very likely be reduced to DER without harm if needed. 

So in general, applications that need to tolerate BER should handle that complexity themselves. Maybe share a common shim for a format. But this complexity should remain in those applications instead of being brought into pyca

Dropping checks sounds like the most harmful way of providing compatibility.

comments.author: DemiMarie
comments.body:
> > CMS Advanced Electronic Signatures has signatures over BER-encoded data.
> > It appears that some BSI standards actually require not being complient with DER.
> 
> Not every use-case needs to be supported considering the maintenance burden. I'm sure there are even more bespoke complex use-cases out there that could be found. Looking at CAdES, it also seems like the signature is (very reasonably) over DER not BER, to be deterministic. The outer structure can be BER, thus it can very likely be reduced to DER without harm if needed.

Some countersignatures in CAdES (which is very widely used in Europe) are taken over the original signature, however it happened to be encoded.  Going from BER to DER would corrupt it.  The standard mentions that DER _should_ be used, but that is not a requirement.  One of the goals of CAdES is long-term storage, so I expect that implementations will be expected to support signatures that did not use DER.

> So in general, applications that need to tolerate BER should handle that complexity themselves. Maybe share a common shim for a format. But this complexity should remain in those applications instead of being brought into pyca
> 
> Dropping checks sounds like the most harmful way of providing compatibility.

I think the vast majority of use-cases need to handle full BER.  An implementation that only supports DER is not an implementation of PKCS\#7/CMS or of PKCS\#12, but rather only of a subset of those standards that does not include many uses people have no choice but to use.

Apple code signatures don’t use DER.  Neither do EJBCA or ADCS exports, nor do various other things that people don’t have any chance of changing.  In particular, anything based on BouncyCastle does not use DER.  Unless an application _knows_ that it only needs DER support, then it will need to pull in that shim.

Arguably, RSA Security and the IETF made a mistake when they defined PKCS\#7/CMS and PKCS\#12, but it’s too late to change that.  There’s simply too much data already in the wild that needs to be handled, and the users of pyca/cryptography simply don’t have the ability to change those who produce non-DER data.

comments.author: DemiMarie
comments.body: It’s worth noting that many of the sources of non-DER BER come from national governments, who are _notoriously_ slow to change direction.  Perhaps someday only DER will be relevant, but that will not be for a long time.

comments.author: TaaviE
comments.body:
> Some countersignatures in CAdES (which is very widely used in Europe) are taken over the original signature, however it happened to be encoded. 

> I think the vast majority of use-cases need to handle full BER.

Original signatures which should (not SHOULD) be all DER. Can you reference where they're actually BER (instead of just the "container")? Better yet, maybe examples could be provided.

> Unless an application knows that it only needs DER support, then it will need to pull in that shim.

Which is totally fair and very likely much more suitable for each use-case than trying to provide a generic "kitchen sink". In general not knowing what you need and cryptography aren't a good mix in the first place. In that sense a manual toggle "I want (legacy) BER" would be fair while OSSL fallbacks exist. But again, shouldn't be the default.

title: Fernet constructor taking `bytes` has non-obvious behaviour
need_summary: The developer needed to know whether Fernet can accept a raw 32‑byte key without base64 encoding, and the maintainer answered that the library follows the Fernet spec (https://github.com/fernet/spec) which defines a single base64‑encoded key format.
security_topic: Fernet key format handling and API design
question_text: I would like to create a Fernet object with `bytes` of len 32, without additional base64 en/decode.
answer_text: Fernet implements the specification documented at https://github.com/fernet/spec which defines exactly one key format. Given that the documentation is unambiguous and if you attempt to pass 32-bytes you'll get a clear exception, I'm not sure there's anything to be done here.
thread_text:
ISSUE #12920: Fernet constructor taking `bytes` has non-obvious behaviour
Author: petoknm
Date: 2025-05-17T11:43:30Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
I have a private key in the form of a `bytes` object with len=32. I want to use it to construct `Fernet` object as stated in the documentation.

```
key (bytes or str) – A URL-safe base64-encoded 32-byte key. This must be kept secret. Anyone with this key is able to create and read messages.
```

My expectations from reading docs:
Constructor takes in `bytes | str` so I would assume I can feed it raw 32 bytes in the form of `bytes` or a longer, base64 encoded string that decodes to 32 bytes.

Reality:
Whatever you supply, gets base64 decoded... so I cannot use a raw 32 byte `bytes` object directly... I have to base64 encode it first, only to be base64 decoded in the constructor...

I would like to create a Fernet object with `bytes` of len 32, without additional base64 en/decode.

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @alex 2025-05-17T11:56:42Z:
Fernet implements the specification documented at https://github.com/fernet/spec which defines exactly one key format.

Given that the documentation is unambiguous and if you attempt to pass 32-bytes you'll get a clear exception, I'm not sure there's anything to be done here.
---
[c2] @petoknm 2025-05-17T14:16:56Z:
Thank you for your quick response.

The specification you linked does not dictate the Python API.

The key serialized as `bytes` with len=32 is functionally equivalent to its base64 encoded version... so why would I want to carry around/store/work with a longer key if I can work with a shorter key? If I have to keep track of a lot of keys, the more compact the representation is, the better.

I think having both options is good. That's why I automatically assumed that `bytes` gets treated differently compared to `str`... I expected `str` to be the base64 encoded key and `bytes` to be the raw, unencoded key (because it allows us to have this more compact representation). 

I understand if you don't want to change the existing API's behaviour, so how about a new method?

```py
Fernet.from_raw_key(key_bytes_of_len32: bytes) -> Fernet
```

Currently, I'm fine with a workaround where I base64encode the bytes to form the key... I just think its redundant work, that's all.
---
[c3] @github-actions 2025-05-22T00:00:15Z:
This issue has been waiting for a reporter response for 3 days. It will be auto-closed if no activity occurs in the next 5 days.
---

title: ML-KEM API Design
need_summary: The developer asked if expanded ML‑KEM decapsulation keys should be serializable, and the answer cited a security concern with a reference to the IETF slide on the private‑key war (https://datatracker.ietf.org/meeting/122/materials/slides-122-pquip-the-great-private-key-war-of-25-00).
security_topic: private key serialization requirements for ML-KEM in SSH
question_text: There is a strong desire to not expose expanded decap keys as a serializable type for a variety of reasons (see: https://datatracker.ietf.org/meeting/122/materials/slides-122-pquip-the-great-private-key-war-of-25-00), so I'm interested in what the SSH protocol's requirements are for this. I'm guessing you need to be able to obtain encapsulation keys as raw bytes with no SPKI wrapper, but what else?
answer_text: As expected, there was no requirement to serialize the private key data. So, the fact that this API operates only on the seed and not the expanded key will not be a problem.
thread_text:
ISSUE #12824: ML-KEM API Design
Author: reaperhulk
Date: 2025-04-29T19:03:30Z
Labels: api design
State: closed

[c0]
Here's a strawman, let's discuss.

A few thoughts:
* I don't want to use public/private, but Encapsulation and Decapsulation are quite verbose. I've used Encap/Decap below but we can use the full words if people think it's better.
* I see no reason to support/allow anything other than seed only PKCS8 for both loading and serialization.
* Do we want to support bare seed loading? The current API proposal below does allow it similar to how we do it in Ed/X keys.
* If we support bare seed loading then we should support bare seed serialization. We can repurpose `PrivateFormat.Raw` for this I suppose.
* How do we load PKCS8? We have `load_{pem,der}_{public,private}_key` functions, but if we don't want to use the public/private nomenclature we may want new functions.
* This proposal makes the parameter set a property of the class rather than a value to be passed. We could choose to expose an enum of parameter sets (768 and 1024...maybe 512 if necessary, although it seems no one is implementing that) instead of this. Go has chosen separate concrete interfaces (https://github.com/golang/go/issues/70122) for this and I generally think separate types are a reasonable choice here, although a consequence is that code that supports multiple MLKEM sizes will need to have type signatures like `input: MLKEM768EncapKey | MLKEM1024EncapKey`


```python
class MLKEM768DecapKey:
    @classmethod
    def generate(cls) -> "MLKEM768DecapKey":
        ...

    def decap(self, ciphertext: bytes) -> bytes:
        ...

    def encap_key(self) -> "MLKEM768EncapKey":
        ...

    def private_bytes(
        self,
        encoding: serialization.Encoding,
        format: serialization.PrivateFormat,
        encryption_algorithm: serialization.KeySerializationEncryption,
    ) -> bytes:
        ...

    @classmethod
    def from_seed_bytes(cls, data: bytes) -> "MLKEM768DecapKey":
        ...


class MLKEM768EncapKey:
    def encap(self) -> Tuple[bytes, bytes]:
        """
        Note that this tuple should be shared_secret, ciphertext to match the spec
        """
        ...

    def public_bytes(
        self,
        encoding: serialization.Encoding,
        format: serialization.PublicFormat,
    ) -> bytes:
        ...
```

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @alex 2025-04-29T21:01:37Z:
Thoughts:

a) Overall API design looks fine
b) I'm a bit ambivalent on encap/decap vs. full words. I have easy arguments for both sides of it.
c) Is there a use case for bare seeds? If so, let's do it (since easy), but if there's no concrete usecase, skip for now (easy to add later). I guess there obviously is for encap keys?
d) Yes, seed-only for PKCS8, obviously :-)
e) I think we just reuse the private/public key loading APIs. It's not great, but what can you do.
f) I kind of think the `_bytes()` methods should still be `public`/`private`, since that's really saying "do you need to keep this secret"
---
[c2] @ronf 2025-04-29T21:27:25Z:
Here's the API I'm currently using (which currently wraps around liboqs):

```python
class PQDH:
    """A shim around liboqs for post-quantum key exchange algorithms"""

    def __init__(self, alg_name: bytes):
        """Select the PQ algorithm to use, setting internal methods for keypair, encaps, and decaps"""

    def keypair(self) -> Tuple[bytes, bytes]:
        """Make a new key pair, returning public and private key byte arrays"""

    def encaps(self, pubkey: bytes) -> Tuple[bytes, bytes]:
        """Generate a random secret and encrypt it with a public key, returning secret and cipher text as byte arrays"""

    def decaps(self, ciphertext: bytes, privkey: bytes) -> bytes:
        """Decrypt an encrypted secret using a private key, returning the decrypted secret as a byte array"""
```

What serialization options did you have in mind? I'd want raw bytes in my application, eventually concatenating these bytes with bytes from X25519 or ECDSA and then encoding the combination as an SSH "string" object.

As far as I know, the liboqs library always generates expanded keys in the keypair() call and expects an expanded key in the decaps() call. I don't think it has any support for dealing with seeds. Since the private keys are ephemeral for DH, I don't think supporting seeds would really buy us much for that use case, but I could see later on wanting to have a function to expand a seed to an expanded key.

I still don't quite see how serialization fits in on your decap call. Shouldn't that always return a byte string which matches the byte string passed in to encap (if the key matches)? Neither the public nor private key is returned here.

[c6] @reaperhulk 2025-04-29T21:52:05Z:
There wouldn't be any serialization in decap. The current API proposal isn't stateless, it expects you will have loaded an `MLKEM768DecapKey` and then called `decap` on it with the ciphertext.

There is a strong desire to not expose expanded decap keys as a serializable type for a variety of reasons (see: https://datatracker.ietf.org/meeting/122/materials/slides-122-pquip-the-great-private-key-war-of-25-00 for a bit of context), so I'm interested in what the SSH protocol's requirements are for this. I'm guessing you need to be able to obtain encapsulation keys as raw bytes with no SPKI wrapper, but what else?
---
[c7] @ronf 2025-04-29T22:35:31Z:
SSH requires access to the public key as bytes (1184 bytes long for mlkem768x25519-sha256), along with the 32 byte X25519 public key. It concatenates these and encodes the combination as an SSH string (4 bytes of length followed by concatenated raw key bytes) and sends this public key data in an MSG_KEX_ECDH_INIT message

When the server receives the INIT message, it extracts the public keys and calls encaps() on the PQ public key bytes and gets back a random secret and cipher text. The cipher text (1088 bytes) is combined with X25519 shared bytes (32 bytes) and sent as a concatenated SSH string in a MSG_KEX_ECDH_REPLY message.

The client decrypts the cipher text with decaps() using its private key and creates a shared key made of the random secret and EC shared bytes concatenated and passed into a SHA-256 hash. The server has the same secret bytes and EC shared bytes, and it does the same. There's some other stuff here related to signing with the SSH server's host key, but that's not relevant for this discussion.

I have to admit I don't know the exact formatting of the ML-KEM public key bytes in liboqs, but whatever liboqs returns from its keypair() function is exactly what SSH needed to put on the wire.

That's fine, but I'm not clear on the encap_bytes() and decap_bytes() functions you proposed with serialization arguments. Are those for key serialization? If so, it's confusing to use the same encap/decap name for both purposes.

[c17] @reaperhulk 2026-01-21T16:26:51Z:
That is an immense diff (+8000). I appreciate that it contains roughly everything, but let's strip this down to bare essentials to start reviewing and potentially landing more effectively.

Looking at it a bit, the APIs you've defined for MLDSA are similar to what we did for Edwards curves. However, it is an explicit non-goal of this project to use expanded forms of MLDSA or MLKEM keys -- we will support seed only. Hence, `private_bytes_raw` is not an API we want to support unless it outputs the bare seed. In the proposed API for MLKEM in this thread we have `from_seed_bytes`, which I think you're trying to match with `from_private_bytes`, but due to the expanded vs seed ambiguity I'd prefer the former name for MLDSA as well.

To make some forward progress here I'd suggest the following. Let's pick MLDSA, strip it down to a single key size, and land that. Doing that has this ordering of PRs:
1) Vectors for ML-DSA testing
2) Land impl for boring or aws-lc + docs + tests
3) Followups for other impls.

I just did an interoperability test between this ML-KEM support (using BoringSSL) and a prior implementation I had done on top of liboqs. Everything looks good. The public_bytes_raw() call on the public key is exactly what was needed on the wire by SSH, and so was the ciphertext returned from the encap call. I confirmed that I could exchange the 32-byte secret successfully in both directions.

As expected, there was no requirement to serialize the private key data. So, the fact that this API operates only on the seed and not the expanded key will not be a problem.

[c20] @alex 2026-04-18T21:10:13Z:
Excellent. I think this is all benefitting from teh fact that ML-KEM's cryptographic API is much better designed (with the exception of seed vs. expanded form) and has way fewer parameters than previous cryptographic algorithms (e.g., no multiple representations of signature like ECDSA, or 19 different parameters like RSA PSS).

[c21] @ronf 2026-04-18T21:28:20Z:

[c22] @alex 2026-04-18T21:37:16Z:

comments.body:
There wouldn't be any serialization in decap. The current API proposal isn't stateless, it expects you will have loaded an `MLKEM768DecapKey` and then called `decap` on it with the ciphertext.

There is a strong desire to not expose expanded decap keys as a serializable type for a variety of reasons (see: https://datatracker.ietf.org/meeting/122/materials/slides-122-pquip-the-great-private-key-war-of-25-00 for a bit of context), so I'm interested in what the SSH protocol's requirements are for this. I'm guessing you need to be able to obtain encapsulation keys as raw bytes with no SPKI wrapper, but what else?

comments.author: ronf
comments.body:
SSH requires access to the public key as bytes (1184 bytes long for mlkem768x25519-sha256), along with the 32 byte X25519 public key. It concatenates these and encodes the combination as an SSH string (4 bytes of length followed by concatenated raw key bytes) and sends this public key data in an MSG_KEX_ECDH_INIT message

When the server receives the INIT message, it extracts the public keys and calls encaps() on the PQ public key bytes and gets back a random secret and cipher text. The cipher text (1088 bytes) is combined with X25519 shared bytes (32 bytes) and sent as a concatenated SSH string in a MSG_KEX_ECDH_REPLY message.

The client decrypts the cipher text with decaps() using its private key and creates a shared key made of the random secret and EC shared bytes concatenated and passed into a SHA-256 hash. The server has the same secret bytes and EC shared bytes, and it does the same. There's some other stuff here related to signing with the SSH server's host key, but that's not relevant for this discussion.

I have to admit I don't know the exact formatting of the ML-KEM public key bytes in liboqs, but whatever liboqs returns from its keypair() function is exactly what SSH needed to put on the wire.

comments.author: ronf
comments.body:
> There wouldn't be any serialization in decap. The current API proposal isn't stateless, it expects you will have loaded an MLKEM768DecapKey and then called decap on it with the ciphertext.

That's fine, but I'm not clear on the encap_bytes() and decap_bytes() functions you proposed with serialization arguments. Are those for key serialization? If so, it's confusing to use the same encap/decap name for both purposes.

comments.author: reaperhulk
comments.body:
Dropping this here for my own reference:
* [BoringSSL MLKEM API](https://boringssl.googlesource.com/boringssl/+/refs/heads/main/include/openssl/mlkem.h)
* LibreSSL will be using the boring implementation, but as of 4.1.0 their release notes say `Imported ML-KEM 768 and 1024 from BoringSSL (not yet public API).`
* [OpenSSL KEM API](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man7/EVP_PKEY-ML-KEM/#provider-configuration-parameters)
* [aws-lc KEM API](https://github.com/aws/aws-lc/blob/cddf0ecd56a433497c588d3b5782a5aa9629c077/crypto/fipsmodule/kem/README.md)

All of these will need to be supported in `rust-openssl` to move forward here.

comments.author: frasertweedale
comments.body:
Hello @reaperhulk, @alex, et al.  I'm an engineer at Red Hat and I'm assigned to work toward ML-DSA and ML-KEM support in python-cryptography, aiming to deliver in the first half of 2026.  I had a sync with @simo5 - I believe he was in some earlier discussions, and he conveyed (at a high level) some of the expectations in this project.  These include:

1. delivering support for OpenSSL backend + one additional backend (e.g. BoringSSL or aws-lc).  This is to ensure that the API design and implementation approach are compatible with multiple backends, and we don't accidentally do something OpenSSL-specific.  In terms of which additional backend(s), does the project have any preference?

2. Proper and proactive agreement on APIs and implementation approach.

3. 100% code coverage.

For Red Hat, ML-DSA is the higher priority and I want to work toward delivering that first.  (I did not see a github issue for ML-DSA so I will make a new one).  Is addition of ML-DSA separately and prior to ML-KEM acceptable for you?  (ML-KEM design discussion can proceed in any case).

(For the avoidance of doubt, SLH-DSA is not a priority for us right now.)

Are there any other things that need to be discussed/agreed or that you want to make me aware of, before I dive into the work?

Fraser

comments.author: reaperhulk
comments.body:
That is an immense diff (+8000). I appreciate that it contains roughly everything, but let's strip this down to bare essentials to start reviewing and potentially landing more effectively.

Looking at it a bit, the APIs you've defined for MLDSA are similar to what we did for Edwards curves. However, it is an explicit non-goal of this project to use expanded forms of MLDSA or MLKEM keys -- we will support seed only. Hence, `private_bytes_raw` is not an API we want to support unless it outputs the bare seed. In the proposed API for MLKEM in this thread we have `from_seed_bytes`, which I think you're trying to match with `from_private_bytes`, but due to the expanded vs seed ambiguity I'd prefer the former name for MLDSA as well.

To make some forward progress here I'd suggest the following. Let's pick MLDSA, strip it down to a single key size, and land that. Doing that has this ordering of PRs:
1) Vectors for ML-DSA testing
2) Land impl for boring or aws-lc + docs + tests
3) Followups for other impls.

I just did an interoperability test between this ML-KEM support (using BoringSSL) and a prior implementation I had done on top of liboqs. Everything looks good. The public_bytes_raw() call on the public key is exactly what was needed on the wire by SSH, and so was the ciphertext returned from the encap call. I confirmed that I could exchange the 32-byte secret successfully in both directions.

As expected, there was no requirement to serialize the private key data. So, the fact that this API operates only on the seed and not the expanded key will not be a problem.

comments.author: alex
comments.body: Excellent. I think this is all benefitting from teh fact that ML-KEM's cryptographic API is much better designed (with the exception of seed vs. expanded form) and has way fewer parameters than previous cryptographic algorithms (e.g., no multiple representations of signature like ECDSA, or 19 different parameters like RSA PSS).

comments.author: ronf
comments.body:
Agreed!

On that note, has there been any consideration for adding SNTRUP support to PyCA? It has basically an identical API, and it has been providing quantum-resistant crypto in SSH since OpenSSH 8.0 released in 2019, dating back to before ML-KEM was selected as the new standard. Both SNTRUP and ML-KEM are supported by liboqs, so I'm actually sharing a wrapper between those today in AsyncSSH, but at some point it would be nice to drop liboqs as an additional dependency.

title: Cryptography parsed a CRL file with the authorityCertSerialNumber set to 0.
need_summary: The developer asked whether parsing an authorityCertSerialNumber of 0 violates RFC5280 and constitutes a bug, and the maintainer replied it is intentional and allowed, referencing issue #10247.
security_topic: validation of authorityCertSerialNumber zero value in CRL parsing
question_text: I have a CRL file where the authorityCertSerialNumber field in the AKI extension is set to 0. Cryptography successfully parsed the authorityCertSerialNumber field without any errors. However, according to RFC5280, the authorityCertSerialNumber field stores the certificate serial number, which must be a positive integer. So, is this a bug?
answer_text: Yes, it's fairly intentional. We also allow negative serial numbers (both there, and for certificate's serial numbers), as a result of a large number of certs in the ecosystem still. See #10247.
thread_text:
ISSUE #12748: Cryptography parsed a CRL file with the authorityCertSerialNumber set to 0.
Author: onepeople158
Date: 2025-04-09T14:14:59Z
Labels: x509
State: closed

[c0]
Version:
cryptography-44.0.2

Hello Developer:
I have a CRL file where the authorityCertSerialNumber field in the AKI extension is set to 0. Cryptography successfully parsed the authorityCertSerialNumber field without any errors. However, according to RFC5280, the authorityCertSerialNumber field stores the certificate serial number, which must be a positive integer.So, is this a bug?

Code:
```
from cryptography.x509 import load_pem_x509_crl, load_der_x509_crl
from cryptography.x509 import ExtensionNotFound
import sys

def load_crl(file_path):
    with open(file_path, "rb") as f:
        crl_data = f.read()
    try:
        crl = load_pem_x509_crl(crl_data)
    except ValueError:
        crl = load_der_x509_crl(crl_data)
    return crl

def print_crl_issuer(file_path):
    crl=load_crl(file_path)
    aki_extension = None
    try:
        for ext in crl.extensions:
             if ext.oid == x509.oid.ExtensionOID.AUTHORITY_KEY_IDENTIFIER:
                    aki=ext.value
                    print(aki.authority_cert_issuer)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error parsing CRL: {e}")

file_path = 'crl_aki_serial_0.der'
print_crl_issuer(file_path)
```

title: Documentation: Add an example how to sign/encrypt/sign and encrypt an email
need_summary: The developer needed an example of how to sign and encrypt emails with the cryptography library, and the answer provided a concrete reference to the envelope package (https://github.com/CZ-NIC/envelope) that implements email signing and encryption.
security_topic: example for email encryption using cryptography library
question_text: It would be great to have an authoritative example how to send encrypted emails with cryptography, there are a lot of outdated examples for deprecated packages on the internet each making the world a little less safe.
answer_text: [envelope](https://github.com/CZ-NIC/envelope) is a Python package that implements email signing and encryption on top of cryptography, a link to that package may suffice.
thread_text:
ISSUE #12657: Documentation: Add an example how to sign/encrypt/sign and encrypt an email
Author: dirkgomez
Date: 2025-03-21T07:04:10Z
Labels: documentation
State: open

[c0]
9 andhttps://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/10664, both of which seem to have not really been resolved.


My assumption is: it is possible to sign/encrypt/sign and encrypt emails with cryptography, sources: https://m2crypto.readthedocs.io/en/latest/howto.migration.html#signing or https://cryptography.io/en/latest/hazmat/primitives/asymmetric/serialization/#cryptography.hazmat.primitives.serialization.pkcs7.PKCS7EnvelopeBuilder 

Yet I'm struggling to properly send encrypted emails with cryptography and Python standard modules. The building blocks are there, I can encrypt and send emails, yet the result isn't production ready:

* they contain headers and the content-type information
* long lines are broken up into multiple lines
* no subject

Here's how my code currently looks like:

```
    message["Subject"] = subject
    message["To"] = recipient
    message["From"] = from
    message["Sender"] = sender

    message.set_content(content)
    if attachments:

        for attachment in attachments:
            message.add_attachment(
                base64.b64decode(attachment.content),
                maintype="application",
                subtype="octet-stream",
                filename=attachment.name,
            )

    options = [pkcs7.PKCS7Options.Text]
    encrypted_content = (
        pkcs7.PKCS7EnvelopeBuilder()
        .set_data(message.as_bytes())
        .add_recipient(certificate)
        .encrypt(serialization.Encoding.SMIME, options)
    )

    encrypted_message = BytesParser().parsebytes(encrypted_content)

    encrypted_message["Subject"] = subject
    encrypted_message.set_payload(encrypted_content)

```
It would be great to have an authoritative example how to send encrypted emails with cryptography, there are a lot of outdated examples for deprecated packages on the internet each making the world a little less safe.

need_summary: The developer asked for an estimate on when post‑quantum algorithm support (e.g., ML‑KEM) will be added, and the maintainer responded that there is no timeline but expressed hope for ML‑KEM in the next release and referenced https://cryptography.io/en/latest/statements/state-of-openssl/ as a source.
security_topic: estimate for adding post-quantum cryptography support
question_text: could you provide some estimate on when we could expect addition of support for PQC algorithms?
answer_text: I'll give you three answers, you can decide which one you like best :-) 1. As an OSS project developed in our free time, we don't offer timelines. 2. It's something we're actively interested in, and I'm hopeful we'll have ML-KEM at least in our next release. 3. You might not be happy, because that support is likely to be only for users on (some combination of) LibreSSL, BoringSSL, or AWS-LC and not OpenSSL. Please see https://cryptography.io/en/latest/statements/state-of-openssl/ for context.
thread_text:
ISSUE #12610: OpenSSL 3.3, 3.4, 3.5 features to expose
Author: h-vetinari
Date: 2025-03-12T23:44:15Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
This is a continuation of #9795 for newer versions. The points here are simply harvested from the feature list in openssl's [`NEWS.md`](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/master/NEWS.md), not all of them are necessarily applicable to cryptography (but I don't know how to make that determination, so I opted to err on the side of completeness). Please feel free to prune/edit/expand the list as you see fit.

* OpenSSL v3.3
  * [x] Added a new EVP_DigestSqueeze() API. This allows SHAKE to squeeze multiple times with different output sizes.
  * [x] New atexit configuration switch, which controls whether the OPENSSL_cleanup is registered when libcrypto is unloaded.

* OpenSSL v3.4

* OpenSSL v3.5
  * [ ] Support for PQC algorithms
    * [ ] ML-KEM (#12824)

title: Support for Code Signing Certificates to x509.verification
need_summary: The developer needed to know how to validate a code‑signing certificate chain with cryptography’s new ExtensionPolicy API, which is available only in the unreleased main branch (see merged issue #11165 and the test example at github.com/pyca/cryptography/.../test_verification.py#L383).
security_topic: code signing certificate verification using cryptography x509 API
question_text:
I want to use cryptography to validate a certificate chain of a signing certificate. But the x509.verification can only support server and client certificates.

Did I miss anything, or is there a work around to get that working. For a first step it would be okay for me to just validate the certificate chain to a root. The check if the leaf certificate has the correct KU and EKU can be done manually, but Path validation is tedious and error prone to implement myself.
answer_text:
For examples on how the ExtensionPolicy API can be used, you can reference the tests, for example this one:
https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/5e899038809a0895f75423524dcb832a580b77de/tests/x509/verification/test_verification.py#L383

### There are two main differences between a ClientVerifier and a ServerVerifier:
1. A ServerVerifier is built with a specific `subject`, and the verification will fail if the certificate doesn't contain a SAN extension which matches the `subject` specified in `build_server_verifier`. So this is intended to be used when you know who the certificate must belong to, which is the case when connecting to a server via https. In many other cases you don't know the subject in advance. Then ClientVerifier can be used, which doesn't require that the SAN extension contains a specific value.
   Despite not knowing the exact subject, you may still have eg. a whitelist of possible subjects, and after calling `ClientVerifier.verify`, you can access the subjects from the SAN extension via `VerifiedClient.subjects`.

2. The default EE extension policies check the EKU extension. For ClientVerifier, it is required to have the ClientAuth EKU, and for ServerVerifier, ServerAuth. The EKU is not currently user configurable (although this may be exposed later via a method on PolicyBuilder), however you can create a custom extension validator callback and use a custom extension policy that will constrain the EKU in any way you want.

### Why some properties are on `Policy` but not on `PolicyBuilder`
The current `Policy` class is basically a direct mapping to python from a rust struct that contains context required for chain building and certificate verification/validation. The main purpose of the `Policy` class is to expose this context to python extension validation callbacks (as set by `ExtensionPolicy.may_be_present` and similar methods) so that the callbacks can express complex constraints based on these parameters. There wasn't really a per-property decision process on whether to include something there or not, but I don't think it hurts to have extra stuff there since we can't envision every use case. Some of these properties, for example, EKU, as you have noted, can not yet be configured by the user. However they can still be useful, for example you might want to write a verification callback for another extension that makes a decision based on what EKU value is required by the policy.

You are right that this might be a bit confusing currently, and there is a slight leakage of implementation details into the public API. However this could not be reasonably avoided currently I would say, and I would err on the side of the `Policy` class providing access to extra properties rather than trying to predict every use case.

The EKU is not currently user configurable (although this may be exposed later via a method on PolicyBuilder), however you can create a custom extension validator callback and use a custom extension policy that will constrain the EKU in any way you want.

### Why some properties are on `Policy` but not on `PolicyBuilder` 
The current `Policy` class is basically a direct mapping to python from a rust struct that contains context required for chain building and certificate verification/validation. The main purpose of the `Policy` class is to expose this context to python extension validation callbacks (as set by `ExtensionPolicy.may_be_present` and similar methods) so that the callbacks can express complex constraints based on these parameters. There wasn't really a per-property decision process on whether to include something there or not, but I don't think it hurts to have extra stuff there since we can't envision every use case. Some of these properties, for example, EKU, as you have noted, can not yet be configured by the user. However they can still be useful, for example you might want to write a verification callback for another extension that makes a decision based on what EKU value is required by the policy.

You are right that this might be a bit confusing currently, and there is a slight leakage of implementation details into the public API. However this could not be reasonably avoided currently I would say, and I would err on the side of the `Policy` class providing access to extra properties rather than trying to predict every use case. Maybe there's something to be said about the naming - there is a clear parallel between `PolicyBuilder` and `Policy`, but, as @loewexy said, not all properties configurable via the builder are accessible on `Policy` and vice versa. I don't have any good ideas on how to improve this currently, but maybe we _can_ come up with a better name for `Policy`

comments.author: deivse
comments.body:
Oh yeah, and regarding having the extension policies or the store as properties on `Policy`:
1. For the extension policies, I don't see a strong use case currently, and it would require creating a mapping from rust to python (which currently is only the other way around), which is not something you want to do, trust me 😄
2. The store is not really part of the `Policy`, since it's potentially specific to verifying a single certificate, whereas a policy (conceptually here, not necessarily the `Policy` class) can be used to verify any number of certificates issued by different CAs.

That second point brings me to a renaming idea, which might actually make sense, but it's a breaking change unfortunately - instead of renaming `Policy` it would maybe make more sense to rename `PolicyBuilder` to something like `VerifierBuilder`. It sounds worse, but does make more sense conceptually imo, since what you actually build with it are verifiers, not policies, and you can also set things that are not part of the policy - the certificate store. Any thoughts on this, @alex, @reaperhulk?

DISCLAIMER: I sound pretty confident about some of these things here, but I'm not a core contributor here, so take what I say with a small grain of salt 😄 I just happened to work on this feature.

title: verify_directly_issued_by compares encoded subjects rather than subject values
need_summary: The developer asked whether verify_directly_issued_by should compare issuer/subject values using StringPrep per RFC 5280 rather than ASN.1 encoding, and the maintainer answered that the library follows the CABF Baseline Requirements (section 7.1.4.1) and RFC 5280, confirming the current behavior and indicating a bias against implementing StringPrep.
security_topic: policy on distinguished name comparison in certificate verification
question_text: Could there be an option to use StringPrep based comparison with adequate warnings about it being disfavoured?
answer_text: The consensus among the X.509 folks I've spoken to is that the RFC5280 StringPrep behavior is extremely disfavored at this point, so we're going to have a strong bias against implementing that.
thread_text:
ISSUE #12361: verify_directly_issued_by compares encoded subjects rather than subject values
Author: wkral-netlync
Date: 2025-01-29T20:22:07Z
Labels: waiting-on-reporter, Stale
State: closed

[c0]
In a certificate being verified the issuer name attributes are encoded using PRINTABLESTRING, while the issuer cert encodes it's subject name attributes with UTF8STRING. When using `verify_directly_issued_by` an exception is thrown:
```
ValueError: Issuer certificate subject does not match certificate issuer.
```

The comparison is done with the ANS.1 encoded values:
https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/ad537914d55373f00c1be3eb7aaea1851859d042/src/rust/src/x509/certificate.rs#L331-L339

I think that the comparison should follow the rules outlined in [RFC 5280 Section 7.1 Internationalized Names in Distinguished Names](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5280#section-7.1) which would ignore the ASN.1 encoding and compare the values.

The cause of the exception was difficult to find since two `x509.Certificate` objects subjects do compare positively in python:

```python
untrusted.issuer == issuer.subject  # True
```

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @alex 2025-01-29T23:17:00Z:
The behavior we have there matches what's in the CABF BRs https://cabforum.org/working-groups/server/baseline-requirements/documents/TLSBRv2.0.4.pdf at 7.1.4.1
---
[c2] @wkral-netlync 2025-01-30T18:56:40Z:
Reading through that portion of the CABF spec the relevant section seems to be:

>For each CA Certificate in the Certification Path, the encoded content of the Subject
>Distinguished Name field of a Certificate SHALL be byte‐for‐byte identical among all
>Certificates whose Subject Distinguished Names can be compared as equal according to RFC
>5280, Section 7.1, and including expired and revoked Certificates.

It clearly says byte-for-byte identical, but I find it slightly odd that it points to the same portion of the RFC that I did which states:

> Conforming implementations MUST use the LDAP StringPrep profile
> (including insignificant space handling), as specified in [[RFC4518](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4518)],
> as the basis for comparison of distinguished name attributes encoded
> in either PrintableString or UTF8String.

It seems a bit contradictory to me.

The CABF spec seems to only cover TLS Server Certificates, but there are many other x509 certificate chain use cases, and the reason I've been trying to use `verify_directly_issued_by` is because the `x509.verification` API only covers server certs and client certs and checks for the key usage attributes. I'm working with JWS [RFC 7515](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7515) and CMS [RFC 5652](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5652) and I think there are probably several other cases. It would be useful if cryptography could be used more generally for certificate chain verification without having to go deep into the hazmat portion of the library. This is especially true with PyOpenSSL having deprecated all of the x509 portions of it's library in favour of cryptography.
