The consensus among the X.509 folks I've spoken to is that the RFC5280
StringPrep behavior is _extremely_ disfavored at this point, so we're going
to have a strong bias against implementing that.

title: Verify Certificate Chain Without Trust Store
need_summary: The developer needed to know how to obtain intermediate certificates for chain verification, and the answer pointed to Python's ssl.SSLSocket.get_unverified_chain documentation as the concrete source.
security_topic: retrieving TLS intermediate certificates in Python
question_text:
Okay, fair enough. Is there a way to get the intermediates using Cryptography? So far I've seen this:
```leaf = load_pem_x509_certificate(ssl.get_server_certificate((subject, 443)).encode())```
But as far as I can tell, that only returns the leaf, and not whatever intermediates the server might also be presenting.
answer_text:
Getting the intermediates from the TLS handshake is going to be a question of your TLS libraries API.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/ssl.html#ssl.SSLSocket.get_unverified_chain is probably what you want

title: Wrong type annotation for is_signature_valid
need_summary: The developer needed to know that the type signature for `CertificateRevocationList.is_signature_valid` is correct because a certificate can contain a public key not valid for issuing, and they should refer to the Cryptography library’s `CertificateIssuerPrivateKeyTypes` documentation (https://cryptography.io/en/latest/hazmat/primitives/asymmetric/#cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.types.CertificateIssuerPrivateKeyTypes).
security_topic: type annotation mismatch for cryptography public key validation
question_text: I think the mistake is in the type annotations (unless I am doing something wrong, of course).
answer_text:
Unfortunately, that's correct.

A certificate can _carry_ a public key that's not valid for issuing certificates, and the type signatures reflect this.

You can use https://cryptography.io/en/latest/hazmat/primitives/asymmetric/#cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.types.CertificateIssuerPrivateKeyTypes to check for this (either with `typing.cast()` or an `isinstance` check.)

title: Build failure on Mariner (azurelinux) because of unsupported cipher `chacha20_poly1305`
need_summary: The developer asked if the cryptography package can be built without ChaCha20 support (related to CVE‑2023‑49083) and the maintainer replied it would take a few hours, citing the CI workflow (https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci.yml#L37) and the cipher registry source (https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/main/src/rust/src/backend/cipher_registry.rs#L126) as concrete references.
security_topic: effort estimate for supporting no‑chacha OpenSSL build configuration
question_text: In any case, can I get a rough estimate of how complicated this is going to be for someone that isn't familiar with the codebase?
answer_text:
I'd probably estimate it at a couple of hours for someone not familiar with the codebase. I can give you a brief tour of what's involved:

- https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci.yml#L37 is the CI job that you can update to test no-chacha
- https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/main/src/rust/src/backend/cipher_registry.rs#L126 are some examples of using an OSSLCONF
- src/rust/Cargo.toml has some metadata that'd need to be updated

So the main task would be finding the places that rely on chacha being available and adding the appropriate `cfg()` handling.

([source](https://github.com/microsoft/azurelinux/blob/2a17e481fe1b06e3e7980d5d4d32d8a15ad97879SPECS/python-cryptography/0001-remove-openssl-cipher-Cipher-chacha20_poly1305.patch))

[c1] @alex 2025-01-09T15:46:33Z:

Yes, as per the `openssl.spec` file found here: https://github.com/microsoft/azurelinux/blob/2.0/SPECS/openssl/openssl.spec
It seems that they use `./config no-chacha` (among other things).
For mariner 2.0 (which we currently use), they use `cryptography` version `3.3.2` and then apply a patch to solve `CVE-2023-49083` ([here](https://github.com/microsoft/azurelinux/blob/2.0/SPECS/python-cryptography/CVE-2023-49083.patch)).
For azurelinux (mariner 3.0), they use `cryptography` version `42.0.5` and apply a patch to remove the relevant Rust code ([here](https://github.com/microsoft/azurelinux/blob/3.0/SPECS/python-cryptography/0001-remove-openssl-cipher-Cipher-chacha20_poly1305.patch)).
We install and use our own packages, so we don't use the `cryptography` package that they have installed, but we can't install the version we want (`43.0.1` currently).
